column121: On taxi out from gate XX we were cleared to spot XX. We switched over to ground and were called almost immediately and given clearance to taxi to runway 17R; at the end of the clearance we were told to give way to another aircraft taxing north bound on kilo. The sun was coming up and shining directly into the cockpit impairing visibility. The fo had his window shade up with his attached visor on his window. The combination of grounds give way clearance at the end of his taxi clearance; the sunlight and visors being up made it difficult to see the north bound traffic. This resulted in an abrupt stop to avoid pulling out in front of the oncoming aircraft. After the aircraft passed we continued on our clearance and taxied out. I called back to the flight attendants and asked if everyone was ok with that abrupt stop. My Purser; informed me that another FA had fell over and hit the cockpit door. I asked to talk to her and she informed me that she hit her arm but was ok. She stated she would put some ice on it but was fine to continue with the flight. I asked her again if she was sure she was ok and she repeated that she was fine. Based on her inputs I continued the flight. All other flight attendants and passengers did not report any issues or injuries. During cruise I checked in with her again during our restroom break; she informed me she put ice on her arm and was feeling better. My overall impression of her upon our discussion based on her stance; body language and inflection was she appeared to be fine and performing her duties normally. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Cause: A combination of factors; Ground gave the clearance to taxi out and at the end of the clearance told us to give way. At this point the aircraft was coming up on us and we had forward moment as ground had cleared us to taxi; plus the direct sunlight from the morning sun was some what blinding; which led to the additional visors places on the forward windows which made it harder to see traffic approaching from the right.

column121: My student and I were entering Fernandinha Beach Municipal (FHB) for closed traffic touch and go operations. My student executed good radio calls. He reported 5 miles out with intentions; again over the field; execution of right teardrop for left downwind of RWY 9; again on downwind with intention; base; and final. There was an aircraft on a base to final turn who we had in sight; and Aircraft Y who reported approaching from the south (he actually transitioned north to south of the field). Aircraft Y reported a left downwind for RWY 4 and then changed his approach to final RWY 9 after we had made our final call for RWY 9. As we made calls to figure out where this aircraft was; we got no response. I told my student to execute a go-around because we did not have the traffic in sight. During our execution of the go-around procedure; I witnessed the Aircraft Y wing high; underneath us with about an average separation of 200 feet both vertically and laterally. I made radio calls to ask if they had seen us; and reported them flying directly underneath us; with no response. We exited the pattern to the north and so did Aircraft Y. I; again; made a radio call asking if they were monitoring frequency. When Aircraft Y responded. I asked if he had seen us; to which he replied; I did see you and I am sorry. He proceeded inbound and landed at FHB full stop and we continued maneuvers and then continued with pattern work before heading back to ZZZ. After the flight I was able to review the track and see that Aircraft Y has approached from the north and transitioned to a approach from the south for a final on RWY 31. A runway that intersects RWY 9.

column121: On this day at XA:15 coming into land at ZZZ I had a gear malfunction. Details are listed as follows. On the downwind at my thousand foot markers abeam [runway] XX I preformed my GUMPS checklist to where I lowered my gear and promptly received all three green lights. As I turned my base I verified again by a quick glance as I looked at my control instruments and one more time on short final. As I flared and proceeded to touch down there were no abnormalities. However about 3 seconds later; give or take; my auditory gear horn came on and before I could even remotely react the right wing hit the ground and dug itself into the ground. As the plane went hard right I did full left rudder and managed to keep the plane on the ground. We exited the plane and turned everything off. No other gear collapsed and functioned properly. There were no injuries and the plane received minimal damage to the wing tip. It also bruised the flaps and the ailerons on the right side. This was a great learning experience and even though it was nerve racking my training and flying had prepared me for a situation like this and am very grateful no injuries occurred.

column121: I was working lakeside satellite. Aircraft X wanted an RNAV 36 approach to TME. That information has to [be] passed to the tower. Usually we have a direct line to the tower but for the last several weeks the shout line has been out of service. When the shout line is out of service I call flight data to call the inbound via the telephone number. Usually flight data does not have a problem with that but a couple of controllers do for some reason even though that is a part of flight data job description. While I am working a radar control position I will not call on the telephone line to an outside facility. That is dangerous; a distraction and in the past at other facilities has led to fatal crashes. I called flight data and Person A was working. He told me unable. He has refused to do his job dozens of times when I requested it and nothing appears to be done. I then called the Controller in Charge (CIC) to notify them and for them to call my inbound.Recommendation: First there should always be urgency when communication equipment is out of service and a rush to get it fixed as soon as possible. This is a safety issue. We need direct communication with towers that we work approach for. Flight data controllers need to be trained properly and corrected when they refuse to do their job. Radar control position should never be expected to call an outside facility on a phone line. That is dangerous. This has to be addressed.

column121: There were three POB (Persons on Board). Left [seat] is a CPL (Commercial Pilot License) with IR (Instrument Rating) and CFII getting an IPC (Instrument Proficiency Check) in a Piper Navajo. In the right seat is a CFII performing the IPC. In the back seat is the primary operator of the aircraft but does not have instructor certificate. All pilots have the CPL.The pilot flying (left) performed multiple approaches under a view limiting device in VMC. During the first approach; ILSXX into ZZZ noticed the right landing gear light would not illuminate. The pilot in the back seat stated they heard the gear lock and it is a known issue that the right downlink switch is not calibrated correctly and sometimes sticks. The IPC continued with a missed approach. The next approach was the ILSXY into ZZZ. The same issue persisted and the gear was cycled multiple times with no apparent issues other that the right main landing gear light. The light was tested (push) with no defects noted. The pilot flying executed a missed approach.The third approach was the VOR-A into ZZZ1. During the circling approach; the same landing gear issue persisted and the IPC would continue for one more approach into ZZZ1. During the final approach; the pilot monitoring simulated a loss of power in the right engine. The pilot flying maintained control and continued the approach. The landing gear was cycled down with the right MLG light not illuminating. The pilot flying noticed the nose landing gear light was now not illuminating and the mirror check revealed the NLG was not fully extended. The gear was cycled two more times with no effect and the gear not retracting. A missed approach was executed and the pilot flying climbed to 2500' MSL. The pilot in the back was notified of the defect and elected to take control. The pilot monitoring (right seat) took control of the aircraft while the pilot from the back swapped seats with the pilot in the left seat. Out of an abundance of caution; the two more experienced pilots would helm for the abnormality. The current pilot flying performed the appropriate checklist items and manually extended the gear till the nose gear light illuminated. The right MLG light still would not illuminate. No emergency or priority request was made. The pilots flying now performed a min speed landing. and the landing gear did not collapse. Upon shutdown; a substantial amount of hydraulic fluid was noticed by the aircrew on the left inboard trailing edge of the aircraft and the left wheel well was dripping with fluid. It appeared a flexible hydraulic line had been breached and there was substantial fluid loss.

column121: I was on an eastern heading in the practice area after maneuvering over confined space for a period of about 30 minutes. I was setting up to perform a chandelle maneuver to the left. When scanning for traffic before doing the maneuver; I spot a low wing aircraft on a northern heading about 200-300 feet below me and about a half mile to my right. I then start a climb in order to avoid a mid-air collision. The other aircraft continued on their northern heading. Once I landed at LAF; I had a conversation with the other aircraft's pilot to ensure that both parties noticed the threat. I believe a contributing factor to the incident was my complacency in the fact that I started to become too comfortable in the small section of airspace I was maneuvering in. Even though I was clearing the area; before and while performing maneuvers; I was not looking long enough to see any traffic from further distances away. One thing that I think could help prevent this type of incident from occurring in the future would be to have a practice area radio communications frequency. I know in other parts of the country this exists and I believe that the surrounding practice areas around LAF would benefit from such a tool.

column121: Around XA:30 on Day 1; while conducting traffic pattern work; a student and I were cleared to take off on XXR and told to make right closed traffic. I did not catch the ATC instruction to 'follow traffic;' only the takeoff clearance and right traffic instruction. In the upwind and upon reaching 700 feet; the student began a right turn. Immediately upon rolling onto the crosswind; we gained sight of traffic on the downwind at the same time ATC called to asked if we had the downwind traffic in sight. I immediately took the flight controls and made a left turn towards the upwind to avoid traffic and reported traffic in sight. I continued in the upwind until ATC advised to turn right and enter the downwind; follow traffic and advise the traffic in sight. We reported the downwind traffic in sight; made a right turn into the downwind to rejoin. On the downwind; we were cleared to land on XXR. After landing; we taxied back to the ramp; shut down and debriefed. I debriefed the situation with the student and made sure to emphasize the importance of maintaining vigilance in the traffic pattern and scanning for traffic. I made it known that I wasn't upset with them and that it was a huge lesson for me and for the student as well. As an instructor; I am trusted to stay vigilant; pay full attention to every radio call and ask ATC for clarification if unsure. I have done a lot of reflecting on this occurrence and went back and listened to the ATC audio recording to figure out how all of this happened. I was pretty shaken up afterwards and still keep asking myself 'How can a 1;000 hour pilot let something like that occur?' I believe a large contributing factor to this incident was fatigue and inadequete nutrition and hydration. I had spent the entire day before (Day 0) volunteering for a non-profit as a pilot. That day had been long and involved extensive waiting on the ground for thunderstorms with insufficient food and water. I believe that had lingering effects on me that night and into the next day (the day of the occurrence). I woke up the next morning feeling a little tired; but thought I felt well enough to fly and work. Feeling rushed that morning; I also did not pack a lunch that morning like I normally do. I refilled my water once that day; but I don't think I was drinking enough. Knowing it was a 90 degree day and I had multiple activities scheduled; I should have taken extra care to hydrate and make sure I was getting enough food. Over all this occurrence has been very eye-opening for me and has taught me huge lessons. One is the paramount importance of remaining vigilant during traffic pattern instructional flights. The other is the importance of checking myself with the IMSAFE checklist that we all preach. It is hugely apparent that the consequences of not doing so can potentially be deadly! I take full responsibility and realize the seriousness of the situation. I wish to use this as a learning moment for myself and my student. Moving forward; I plan to take at an absolute minimum 1 day off of flying completely every week so that I can rest and ensure I am completely present for each and every flight operation and prevent anything like this from ever reoccuring.

column121: While in VMC cruise at FL370; ECAM HYD Y RSVR LO LVL and HYD Y ENG PUMP 2 LO PR annunciated. CA remained PF and took the radios while I worked the blue to do" items. We shut down the PTU (Power Transfer Unit) and Y ENG 2 PUMP per the ECAM and verified that HYD status page showed no quantity in yellow system. CA notified dispatch via ACARS to call on radio and requested priority handling with ATC. I accomplished landing distance calculations and reviewed FM (Flight Manual) non-normal notes and cautions. We transferred control while CA phone patched with dispatch. We determined with dispatch to continue to original destination and dispatch provided landing distance calculations which correlated to my manual calculations. We started an enroute descent with ATC and CA provided the FAs a brief then briefed the pax (passengers) while I got landing ATIS. We came together again to brief the approach and landing considerations; as well as final understanding of how the loss of yellow system would affect landing. We verified that all ECAM and normal checklists were complete and CA accomplished an ILS approach in VMC to a normal landing. Per ECAM status page (APPR PROC blue to do) we turned the Y ENG 2 PUMP back on after extending FLAPS 2 and kept it on until engine shutdown. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) followed us down the runway and on taxi to the gate. We shutdown normally; closed the situation with ground control and deplaned pax through the jetbridge. Fire Chief came aboard and told us we had a significant leak from the center fuselage area and our tires were "shiny."  We thanked him for the support; debriefed in the cockpit; and after the pax were deplaned; debriefed with the FAs. CA called dispatch and Chief Pilot; and we spoke with company mechanics on site as they evaluated the issue."

column121: Departed LAX on DOTSS2.CLEEE. Prior to CLEEE; ATC informed us of possible wake turbulence from a departing A330. We had a direct tailwind at 7 knots and climbing at nearly the same rate as the A330. As we were locating the position of the aircraft; we hit the wake turbulence. We discussed a right deviation or direct PKE; but ATC was already moving the A330 on a northerly track. The autoflight system then displayed autopilot roll authority. I disconnected the autopilot and auto throttles and verbalized the upset; which reached roughly 45 degrees of bank. The FO acknowledged the upset. I slowly rolled the aircraft back to wings level to prevent injury to the flight attendants; who were up at the time. I also made a PA for the flight attendants to take their jump seats; in case we had another encounter. We then increased our rate of climb to stay at or above their altitude. After reporting the issue; ATC informed us the A330 was now on a more northerly route and eventually gave us direct to location X. No further issues were encountered and no injuries or difficulties were reported by the flight attendants.

column121: Approach and landing were normal onto runway 36R in CLT. We were instructed to taxi via J" to J4 where we entered the ramp. Ramp control cleared us to the gate which at this point was almost a straight ahead path into our assigned gate; XXX. As we approached the gate I remember stating that [aircraft type] is posted on the DGS system and that we were aligned with the center line for the XXX gate. As we moved down the centerline my attention was focused on the DGS screen. When we were within approximately 10 feet on the stopping point I heard the First Officer say someone on the ramp outside his window is telling us to stop. I brought the aircraft to a stop and set the parking brake. He then told me that they wanting the engines shut down. As instructed both engines were shut down. I asked the F/O to please open his window to see if he could tell what was happening. He said that a truck was very close to the airplane. column121: Approach control began vectoring us for the visual XXL. As we started to slow down and configure; the flap handle was moved from 1 to 5. Shortly after; we realized we had a problem: the flaps appeared stuck; indicating less than 1. With the handle at 5; I was the pilot monitoring; I requested to cancel the approach and received vectors for a box pattern to troubleshoot. ATC climbed us to 3;000 feet to give us room to work.The First Officer was the pilot flying. Once we reached 3;000 feet; I requested priority handling; stating our fuel and souls on board; and advised that we would need about 20 minutes to work through the various checklists. Knowing these procedures can be lengthy; I felt comfortable because the weather in ZZZ was perfect and we had plenty of gas; including an alternate of Indianapolis; so I was not pressed for fuel and knew we could take our time.I opened the QRH to 'Trailing Edge Flap Asymmetry.' We had no abnormal lights in the flight deck; but the flap indicator showed a slight split with the needles stuck between 0 and 1. The checklist directed us to return the flap handle to UP. As we began that checklist; the flap indicator stopped showing a split. We realized we no longer had an asymmetry; and since that checklist would have required a landing at an extremely high speed which we felt wasn't appropriate for the situation we opted to look for other QRH options.We settled on 'Trailing Edge Flap Disagree.' We felt this was the correct procedure; so we extended the flaps via the alternate flap extension method. Everything progressed normally with no asymmetry or abnormal lights; and we prepared for a flaps 15 landing as directed by the QRH.Once stabilized; I called the flight attendant to brief her on the situation and confirmed it would be a normal landing. I then sent a message to dispatch stating we had requested priority handling; explained the issue; and confirmed we were about to land. I made a PA to the passengers to explain we had a malfunction that required us to work through checklists; and that they should not be alarmed by the presence of emergency vehicles upon arrival. I requested that ATC have ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) standing by and that they follow us to the gate as a precaution.At this point; it was a routine flaps 15 landing. The First Officer was doing a great job; given his previous experience flying this aircraft in the military; I felt comfortable letting him continue the landing while I monitored from a high level. We landed without incident and taxied to the gate; where maintenance personnel met us upon arrival.Cause: We had some uncertainty about whether to use the 'Trailing Edge Flap Asymmetry' or 'Trailing Edge Flap Disagree' checklist. Since the needles had a slight split but we didn't have any abnormal lights; it wasn't immediately clear which path to take. Because these two choices lead to very different QRH procedures; it felt like a tricky situation to navigate. I think the main confusion was around what constituted as flap asymmetry; it was not very clear reading the QRH conditions and objectives header.  Could we look at  putting  some bullet points to consider in the QRH to help clarify.

Possibly consider flying the ILS or RNAV instrument approach instead of the visual in times of known fatigue as this may have mitigated distraction issues.

column121: This report is my best recollection of an altitude deviation that occurred during the OYODA TWO RNAV departure from Henderson Executive Airport (HND).I was operating Aircraft X single-pilot. Due to high summer-like temperatures; the aircraft was operated at a moderately light weight and once airborne; exhibited strong climb performance. Prior to departure; the OYODA TWO RNAV departure was loaded into the G1000 NXi flight management system; and the initial altitude of 6;000 feet was set.The takeoff and initial departure were normal. The aircraft was climbing at approximately 170 KIAS with a climb rate exceeding 2;000 feet per minute. As the aircraft passed through approximately 5;500 feet MSL over the mountainous terrain southeast of Henderson; it encountered a sudden onset of moderate-to-severe turbulence.During the turbulence encounter; my left hand was forced from the control yoke and inadvertently came down on the autopilot disconnect button; resulting in an unexpected autopilot disengagement. At the time; the aircraft was trimmed for a steep climb. I immediately took manual control and applied forward pressure on the yoke while simultaneously reducing power and commanding nose-down electric trim.Despite these corrective actions; the aircraft's climb rate initially increased rather than decreased. At one point; I observed the vertical speed indication at around 3;000 feet per minute. The turbulence required significant attention to aircraft control. It is possible that the aircraft encountered a localized area of strong rising air; although this could not be confirmed.Within approximately 20 seconds; the aircraft climbed through the assigned altitude of 6;000 feet and reached an estimated maximum altitude between 6;600 and 6;800 feet before I was able to arrest the climb and begin descending back toward the assigned altitude. During this period; the aircraft also deviated somewhat from the published lateral departure track as my primary focus was maintaining aircraft control and recovering from the upset.The turbulence remained significant while I worked to reengage the autopilot and reestablish both the assigned altitude and lateral course. Before I could return to 6;000 feet; the departure controller issued an altitude alert. Shortly thereafter; I was instructed to continue climbing to 7;000 feet.The entire event occurred over approximately one minute. I was surprised by the magnitude of the altitude excursion and by my inability to arrest the climb sooner despite immediate corrective action.In retrospect; I should have advised ATC immediately regarding the turbulence encounter. Doing so would have provided important context for the deviation and would have allowed ATC to warn other aircraft operating in the area. My focus on regaining aircraft control; reestablishing the departure path; and complying with assigned altitudes caused me to overlook making that report.

column121: On Day 3 at approximately XA:00; I was operating a DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise under 14 CFR Part 107; conducting a commercial construction-site progress flight at 165 ft AGL. During my planning-stage airspace check three days prior; on Day 0; I observed a published TFR covering the area up to 400 ft AGL; scheduled to become effective Day 1; but not yet in force at the time of my check. I did not log the pending restriction or set a reminder for its effective date; and by the day of the flight I had forgotten it existed.On the day of the flight; my third-party mission-planning software (DroneDeploy) displayed a summary airspace status of 'No Authorization Required' for the planned flight area. I relied on that green status indication and launched. I did not separately verify active TFRs and NOTAMs through official FAA sources before launching. A portion of my planned flight area overlapped the outer edge of the TFR boundary. The operating area is Class G airspace and is normally unrestricted; which contributed to my reliance on the summary status.During my flight; a local law enforcement officer arrived on scene; informed me that an active TFR covered the area; and instructed me to land the aircraft. I landed immediately and complied with all instructions. The airspace incursion was unintentional; and I did not knowingly operate within restricted airspace. The officer issued a verbal warning.Contributing factors: This was primarily a human factor (memory) failure. I learned of the pending TFR during my planning-stage check but did not log it or set a reminder for its Day 1 effective date; and by the flight date I had forgotten it. On the day of the flight; I relied on the third-party application's summary status indicator; which is not an FAA-approved airspace source; rather than verifying through official FAA sources -- so nothing in my day-of process surfaced the restriction or prompted my recollection of it.Corrective actions: Going forward; I will log any pending TFR or NOTAM observed during planning; with its effective date and a calendar reminder; at the time I first see it. I will verify active TFRs and NOTAMs directly through official FAA sources (tfr.faa.gov and the B4UFLY app) immediately before every flight; regardless of any third-party application's status indication. I have added a mandatory day-of official-source TFR/NOTAM check to my preflight checklist. I will not operate at this site for the duration of the TFR period unless authorized through the FAA's Special Governmental Interest (SGI) process.

column121: Climbing out on the ZZZZZX; the captain was PF; and we noticed a cell just west of ZZZZZ. Another build up that was not painting appeared to be over ZZZZZ; but much shorter than the cell to the west. I called the flight attendants via the intercom and told them to remain seated. They confirmed they all were seated. I recall requesting deviations from departure; who would not give them to us at the request of Center.  I was handed over to ZZZ Center and the controller was swamped. I was unable to get a response from the controller. We attempted to avoid the worst of the build up; but still penetrated a building towering cumulus cloud at around 12;000 feet. The plane entered an updraft; banked sharply to the right; and climbed rapidly. The captain grabbed the controls but the autopilot did not disconnect. We were through the build up in 10 seconds. It looked far more benign than the turbulence indicated. We then saw a formation of clouds up ahead; with what appeared to be a mini wall cloud. We could not fly through that. The controller finally told us left deviations only; at which point I refused; because to the right was blue sky and to the left was a scary looking wall cloud. He said there was traffic; and began to talk to other aircraft. I broke back in and said we will be deviating right. The controller than acquiesced to my request. At some point after becoming clear of the storms and we began to rejoin our route; the captain conferred with the flight attendants and we learned of the injuries.Cause: The controller being busy and the busy nature of the ZZZ Bravo and surrounding airspace contributed to this event. I should have advised ATC; but I am not sure if that would have helped for the initial build up penetration; as it was simply too late after getting a controller change. I definitely should have declared one when center was unable to give us deviations as requested. Had the passenger in the lav stayed seated; I do not believe anyone would have been hurt.
column123: During climb out around 10;000'MSL; FO notified flight attendants to remain seated due to turbulence.  Seatbelt sign was on. an area of towering cumulus cloud was visible with a distinct top around 12;000 to 13;000 feet and indistinct cloud layers east and above along our flight path.  Radar returns were only level 1 appropriate for the visible cloud; with higher return levels 30-50 miles south.  Aircraft was slowed to increase climb rate.  I (PF) requested the FO (PM) to ask ATC for deviations west to avoid the area.  FO tried several times to make the request but the controller was busy with multiple deviation requests.  All other aircraft were asked to deviate to the east (not acceptable from our position). As we climbed to the right of the visible cumulous cloud; we entered a non-cumulous cloud.  Within a minute or two (not immediately); the aircraft experienced a rapid climb and rolled right to around 25 degrees.  Positive control was maintained and the Autopilot did not disengage.  AP rolled aircraft back to original heading and shortly after that we entered VMC again. The FA was able to get the controller to allow the deviation; but the controller had to shift arrival aircraft as we entered the arrival corridor.FA 2 advised that a passenger was in the Aft Lavatory at the time.  The FA 2 & 4 directed the passenger to return to his seat.  He ignored their commands.  FA 2 also reported that He; FA 3 and the passenger were experiencing back pain. column121: I was acting as pilot-in-command and flight instructor on a local VFR introductory/sightseeing flight in a Piper PA-11. The flight departed ZZZ and returned to the same airport. The purpose was to provide an introductory flight experience to one passenger/student under visual meteorological conditions. No flight plan was filed; consistent with this routine local operation. I conducted preflight planning and navigation using ForeFlight with a current database.The route proceeded eastbound over ZZZ1 and Location X; followed by a turn back to the west toward ZZZ. Throughout the flight; the aircraft remained under the various shelves of the ZZZ2 Class B airspace. I routinely fly this corridor and normally remain farther south under the higher shelves (typically those with floors at 6;000 ft or 7;000 ft MSL) to maintain extra margin. On this particular flight; with outside air temperature at or above 100°F and reported winds from the south at 10 knots gusting to 18 knots at ZZZ; I observed elevated engine oil temperatures. To assist with engine cooling; I intentionally elected to remain at a lower altitude and track slightly north of my usual path under the Class B shelf with a floor at 4;500 feet MSL near the ZZZ VOR.Shortly after passing the ZZZ VOR westbound; with the engine at reduced power settings to manage the high oil temperature (and with insufficient power available for a sustained climb); the aircraft encountered a strong updraft/thermal. This thermal; likely enhanced by the high ambient temperature; caused an unintended climb that carried the aircraft from below 4;500 feet MSL to approximately 5;000 feet MSL.Upon scanning the altimeter and immediately recognizing the inadvertent penetration of the Class B airspace floor; I promptly reduced power and initiated a gentle descent to return below 4;500 feet MSL. The time spent above the Class B floor was very brief -- estimated at approximately one minute or less. All maneuvering was gentle and smooth; the passenger/student remained unaware of the deviation or the corrective actions. No other aircraft were observed in the vicinity during this period; and there were no observed conflicts with traffic.The aircraft is an antique Piper PA-11 in which I am current and have accumulated over 100 hours. As a professional pilot with approximately 30;000 total flight hours (including extensive airline and general aviation experience); I maintain a strong focus on airspace awareness and have flown this general route many times without issue. This airspace deviation was completely unintentional. It resulted from a combination of my decision to fly a slightly more northerly track at lower altitude/power for engine temperature management; an unexpected strong thermal in that area on a warm evening. Upon recognition of the deviation; immediate and effective corrective action was taken to exit the Class B airspace as quickly and safely as possible.I am submitting this report to contribute to aviation safety. It illustrates how thermal activity on hot days; combined with intentional power/altitude management for engine concerns; can produce brief; inadvertent airspace penetrations even for highly experienced pilots operating in familiar territory. This underscores the importance of maintaining extra lateral margins near Class B shelves and remaining vigilant to altimeter indications during thermal-prone conditions.

column121: C90 STARS system continues to alert controllers via forcing a yellow full or limited data block on arrival scopes any aircraft that is deemed an early decent on an ILS/RNAV final between selected altitudes of approximately 6200-6800 feet outside the 7000 crossing fix on all approaches into ORD. Since implementation this system has created more false alerts than identifying real problems for me. It continues to create distractions and unnecessary nuisance alerts to other controllers; often unrelated to the operation at hand.  Controllers are trained and conditioned that yellow aircraft (yellow data blocks) are special; point outs; or otherwise needing special attention. This is not useful during flow changes; configuration changes; or single/dual runway arrival situations where aircraft can legally and procedural be at those flagged altitudes.  Displaying aircraft unnecessarily as special aircraft via yellow highlight will soon cause controllers to get fatigue from the constant yellow alerts and start ignoring it; and become complacent. We have already seen this throughout the field with the nuisance CA (Conflict Alert) alerts. Specifically; during a two runway arrival operation when the high runway controller can use 5-11000 to join their final/localizer; it is entirely possible an aircraft will (and should) be joining the final at 6000 or higher to allow a base turn ahead of the wider traffic at 5000 for positive separation. Positive separation without nuisance alerts should be absolutely possible.  It should also be noted that random miscellaneous VFR aircraft also show up yellow. But only between the flagged altitudes. This could easily lead a controller to miss other VFRs not within the altitude filter or EDAA box because they are expecting them to be yellow.   Aircraft X was being vectored for an approach to runway 10C in a two runway operation. The W controller was using their assigned altitudes in their assigned airspace but the entire arrival line received a false warning that Aircraft X had descended early while at 6700 feet. This alert was a false positive.  Disable the EDAA entirely as it is an unnecessary distraction in the operation.

column121: Aircraft X routed ..ZZZZZ..ZZZ. I did not issue this clearance; but since it is coded as a rule that controllers match the flight plan to the clearance; I believe it's safe to assume that the aircraft was cleared 'direct ZZZZZ then direct ZZZ;' or 'as filed' if they filed ZZZZZ in their flight plan. Destination airport is within the sector I was working. While coordinating advanced approach information with Aircraft X; I asked what approach they'd like. The pilot responded that they'd like a visual approach; but to follow the course of the RNAV A; which starts at ZZZZZ. I acknowledged this. Later; after giving a pilot's discretion descent to 150; the pilot asked how low I could descend them. I indicated that 110 would be the lowest until ZZZZZ; and that if they proceeded direct to the airport after ZZZZZ; I could descend them to 100. There was a little back-and-forth; and I felt the need to reiterate to the pilot that they would need to proceed direct to the airport after ZZZZZ in order to be able to descend to 100.I did give an instruction to proceed to the airport after ZZZZZ (not as an official clearance; that had supposedly been done already by another controller at an earlier point in time). Much of this discussion; if not all of it; took place while Aircraft X was descending to 150; and it was after at least my first time explaining the altitude situation (if not the second time) that I gave a clearance to 110. At no point did I say 'descend and maintain 100;' only indicated to the pilot that I'd be able to descend them to 100 after ZZZZZ. The pilot read back 110; and the aircraft leveled off at 110 a few miles ahead of ZZZZZ. I took care of some other tasks. Returning to Aircraft X; I saw the aircraft turn at ZZZZZ as their MODE-C-indicated altitude hit 105. There was no MSAW alert due to proximity to the airport. I gave a Low Altitude Alert with an instruction to climb and maintain 110. When I unkeyed; it sounded like someone else was just finishing a transmission too; so I repeated myself. With no response after a few seconds; I changed transmitters and repeated myself once again. Amidst all this; Aircraft X stopped their turn on a heading that was about 10 degrees left of a course direct to the airport... a heading that matched the RNAV-A approach; and which quickly approaches higher terrain.Finally; after the third attempt at a Low Altitude Alert; the pilot responded questioning that they had been cleared to 100 after ZZZZZ. I explained that they were NOT cleared to 100; and reiterated that I had only indicated that I'd be able to descend them to 100 after ZZZZZ; and also explained that their current heading was going into higher terrain; and that the first thing they needed to do was turn towards the airport to remain within the lower MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude). The pilot stated that they were correcting to 110 and turning towards the airport. The aircraft was only below 110 in a 100 MIA polygon for a matter of seconds after ZZZZZ (about 1-2 miles); at which point they entered the 100 polygon. Had they not turned toward the airport; they would have re-entered the 110 MIA polygon; which follows the ZZZZZ..ZZZ course almost exactly parallel; offset to the West by about 3 or 4 miles. Once established on a heading direct ZZZ; still within a 100 MIA and climbing back to 110; I called the airport position to the pilot. They stated it was in sight and I cleared them for a visual approach. It's important for pilots to understand the distinction between a clearance and any other information provided in common language. The most effective preventive measure I could have taken would have been to plan with the pilot to clear them for the RNAV-A approach; and give them a couple minutes before frequency change to get the airport in sight and convert to a visual approach.

column121: The ongoing prohibition of parallel visual approaches at the San Francisco Airport has escalated from an operational inconvenience to a critical safety hazard. The resulting daily Ground Delay Programs (GDP) introduce two unmitigated risks into our system: chronic flight crew fatigue and unpredictable; near-minimum fuel operations.The SFO GDP frequently spans to XA:00 to XQ:00; causing domestic delays ranging from 45 to over 90 minutes. This systematically pushes flight crews to the limits of their Flight Duty Period (FDP); transforming a standard 8 to 10 hour duty day into exhausting 10 to 12 hour marathons. Pilots are regularly forced to fly complex arrivals into a high-density environment after being delayed - sometimes for multiple hours - where fatigue becomes a major factor.This threat materialized on day two of our pairing. Our schedule consisted of a three leg sequence: ZZZZ - SFO; SFO - ZZZZ; and a return to SFO. Both segments into SFO were hit by GDP delays exceeding one hour. The second GDP would have pushed us past our legal 13-hour FDP limit. While the crew desk was able to proactively remove us from the final turn - at considerable financial cost and inconvenience to our customers - many other crews had not timed out. Instead; they are being forced to fly into SFO fatigued; having already exhausted their mental and physical reserves waiting out ground delays.The current SFO configuration also severely compromises fuel planning predictability. Because a GDP of over an hour does not guarantee a clear path upon arrival; clear weather (CAVOK) days now yielding traffic saturation risks usually reserved for low-visibility operations.The severity of this breakdown was demonstrated on our flight from ZZZZ to SFO. The weather at SFO was pristine; endless blue skies with standard westerly winds. Normally; a remaining fuel of 1 hour 15 minutes is sufficient fuel to conduct an approach; handle a go-around; and land with a comfortable 60-minute reserve. Recognizing the SFO volatility; we planned a conservative gate fuel giving us an increased remaining fuel of 1 hour 45 minutes.The fuel preservation effort began immediately on the ground in ZZZZ; where our wheels-up time meant a 15-minute wait at the runway end. We proactively taxied on one engine and shut down the motor during our wait to preserve our margins. However; as we approached SFO our situation deteriorated. While on the BDEGA Arrival; ZOA assigned us a published hold at BGGLO due to traffic saturation on the SFO final approach.We immediately slowed the aircraft and began coordinating our fuel status with dispatch. I determined a bingo fuel of approximately 7;500 lb. before we needed to divert to SMF (1 hour remaining fuel of 5;100 lb. plus 2;300 lb. burn to SMF). We entered the BGGLO hold at 8;900 lb. After just one circuit our fuel had dropped to 8;300 lbs. Recognizing that a third circuit would push us below our diversion threshold; I informed ZOA that the second lap would have to be our final circuit; we either needed to press to SFO or immediately divert to SMF.Fortunately; ZOA released us from the hold with 7;700 lb. remaining. This left us with almost no buffer. To maintain a safe margin at SFO; I wanted a minimum touchdown fuel of 6;300 lb. (1 hour remain fuel of 5;100 lb. plus 1;200 burn to SJC allowing for a go-around at SFO and a diversion to SJC with a 45-minute reserve). I was mentally prepared to declare minimum fuel" and even "emergency fuel" to NORCAL Approach if given any further delay vectors; as the low-speed and low-altitude small box patterns frequently used by ATC during these saturation periods consume fuel at an accelerated rate. I realize 6;300 lb. remaining fuel is higher than Company policy. However I never want to box myself into a position where a go-around will result in an unsafe fuel state.NORCAL managed to sequence us with minimal vectoring; and we landed at SFO with 6;500 lb. While safe; this was significantly belowour flight-planned remaining fuel of 8;281 lb.Despite departing ZZZZ with an extra 30 minutes of fuel on a perfect clear-weather day; the compounding ground and airborne delays brought us to within minutes of an unnecessary diversion. The current SFO arrival restrictions are creating a compound hazard: crews are being kept in the air longer resulting in increasingly narrower fuel margins; all while operating at the tail end of extended and fatigue-inducing duty days. The FAA MUST re-evaluate the prohibition on parallel visuals to restore system predictability and preserve safety margins."

column121: I was the Pilot Flying. The initial climb out on the departure was non-eventful. We were given a climb to 230; and a vector to a waypoint. Once established on a course towards the waypoint; and climbing through 10;000 feet; I requested the autopilot to be selected ON. I watched the Captain press the button; heard the audible click"; and checked that the aircraft was maintaining its climb and heading. At that point I turned my attention to the MCDU (Multipurpose Control Display Unit) to write down the top of climb numbers on my clipboard. As I was writing I was startled by the aural "Bank Angle" warning. I quickly glanced at the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) and noticed that the AP (Autopilot) Mode was not engaged; and we were in a right hand descent; in a steepening bank. I corrected the attitude and airspeed; and the captain engaged the autopilot. We continued the departure and the climb out without further incident.Cause: My failure to ensure the AP cue was populated on the FMA. There was some expectation bias in that regard; as I saw and heard the autopilot button being pressed; and the airplane was trimmed well enough to hold its climb and heading for the few seconds I concentrated on it.Suggestion: The solution to this issue is constantly drilled into us during training events: to pay close attention to the FMA and know for sure what the airplane is being commanded to do. An additional help would be to have the guidance panel lights activated as a secondary cue for what automation is selected on at a given time."

column121: Practice approaches into ZZZ. ZZZ RNAV XX R CIR XY. Past ZZZZZ tower reported winds at 080 @ 8. On final tower reported winds as 030 G 16. Instructor took controls for landing due to crosswind component. Verbalized that go around would be prioritized over landing if approach became unstable at any point. Approach into XY remained stabled throughout descent; airspeed maintained between 60-65 knots and there was a normal descent rate down. Longitudinal axis not fully aligned on landing; causing aircraft to veer left. Right rudder correction to re-establish centerline unable to be put in due to forward inertia. Adding right rudder to regain centerline ran the risk of causing airplane to tip over. Airplane began to weathervane toward grass and go around was unable to be executed due to where the aircraft nose was pointed and how much runway width was available. Held nose wheel up as aircraft veered into the grass and kept off of the brakes. No injuries or visible damage to the aircraft. After aircraft came to a complete stop tower asked if there were any injuries and instructor reported there were no injuries. ATC sent over trucks to get a report and see if tow was needed. Maintenance tow tug came to retrieve aircraft. Probable cause is not enough right rudder for crosswind correction needed. Some ways this could have been mitigated is by applying more right rudder for crosswind correction. I also could have called a go around prior to descent when winds had shifted significantly on final rather than using approach stable by 200' criteria. Another option I could have made could have been to divert to a nearby airport with runways more favorable for winds. ZZZ XX R currently closed and XY was the runway in use.
column123: I had the controls coming in on the approach for XX R circling to XY. We had established prior that if winds reported a higher crosswind; the instructor would take the controls. The entire approach to touchdown was stable. Shortly after touchdown; the plane began to veer to the left without any left inputs and almost felt like it was skidding. We veered off the runway into the grass where we stopped and shut the plane down. Tower had trucks come over and take down some reports and our maintenance came to tow the plane back to the ramp. The plane did not hit anything nor was anybody hurt.

column123: Day 0. Flight XXXX From ZZZ to JFK.  We encountered a significant wake turbulence event about 10 min prior to landing.  The FO was flying and the auto pilot was connected.  The plane rolled hard right.  I grabbed the controls.  I forget if the aircraft disconnected the autopilot or if I did.  The aircraft then rolled hard in the opposite direction.  I turned continuous ignition on. I let ATC know that we encountered wake turbulence.  I initially thought the bank angle was higher than it was.  I told ATC that it was about a 45 degree bank.  After reviewing the flight data it seems the plane banked to 28 degrees and then back the opposite direction to -25 degrees.  We continued the flight as normal.  ATC said we were 7nm in trail of a heavy 777 same altitude.  We requested further separation and continued to land.Cause: Conditions were just right to make the wake of the preceding aircraft stay at altitude for longer.  We were 2nm farther than the required separation.  I don't think anyone did anything wrong.Suggestions: I think the training we have on this type of event is very helpful.  I felt adequately prepared for the situation.

column121: While we were pushing off the gate the flight attendant called and told us a passenger had a lithium battery in her checked suitcase.  I asked the ground crew to stop the push and pull us back in after a conversation with the flight attendant to be completely sure the battery was in the bag and powered on. The ground crew said they needed a ramp manager to pull us back in so we started looking for the ramp manager and I started thinking about all the things that would need to be coordinated; if we were going to open the main door or service door; the security issue of it being in a checked bag not valet; and the other related details.  While we are working on all this other stuff another person comes up and says we need to pull into the gate. So we needed to start an engine and get them disconnected. Since we were initially staying connected the parking brake was never set and no engines were started. Everything started happening quickly and we started an engine and the ground crew asked to disconnect.  With the task saturation and everything being out of order I got distracted and didn't remember we did not set the parking brake when we stopped.  The aircraft began to roll very slightly when the tow bar was being disconnected and I immediately stepped on the toe brakes and set the parking brake.  I checked with the ramp crew to make sure everyone and the plane were okay; then we pulled into the gate and also visually checked the nose gear to be very sure everything looked normal even though the ramp crew assured us everything was normal.Cause: Task saturation during a non normal operation led me to forget a step in the normal tow bar disconnect procedure which was quickly corrected.Suggestions: During the irregular order of operations; I should have not allowed myself to be affected by the sense of urgency to get the flight back to the gate and remove the bag expeditiously so we could be on our way with minimal delay.  I should have slowed everything down; taken my focus from the coordinating and contacting dispatch; ramp; and the flight attendant and put all of that off until we got the aircraft parked.

column123: While taxiing out; had a pitot heat EICAS. Discussed the weather and temperature. Weather was scattered clouds with a temperature of +16 Celsius. Captain did the walk round. We used heading select. LNAV; VNAV; and FLCH lights were all lit up. Both ADIs were giving erroneous information. Clicked off the autopilot and auto throttles. Upset recovery was initiated. Temps were well above freezing with no moisture. Airplane settled down. We initially told center we were non-RVSM; but we could not figure out if it was the INS (Inertial Navigation System) or the airspeed. Controllability check at 10;000 with gear and flaps. No issues. column121: I was providing flight instruction to a private pilot student and conducting takeoffs and landings in the traffic pattern for Runway XX at ZZZ. A student solo aircraft was ahead of us in the pattern; and we elected to extend our downwind leg to allow additional time for that aircraft to clear the runway. We announced our intention to extend downwind on the CTAF.After extending downwind; we turned base and then final. We were established on approximately a 2-mile final when we heard another aircraft report being on a 5-mile final for the same runway. This was the first radio transmission we heard from that aircraft. Prior to turning final; we visually cleared the approach path and did not observe the traffic.I transmitted that we were on a 2-mile final and asked the other aircraft if they had us in sight. The pilot responded that they did. Based on that information; my student and I continued the approach and landing.After touchdown; while we were decelerating and preparing to exit the runway; the other aircraft reported being on short final. We had not yet fully cleared the runway but were in the process of turning off at the next available taxiway. As we initiated the turn; I observed the aircraft; a Cessna Citation; touching down behind us. I took the controls; applied power as necessary; and expedited our runway exit.After landing; the jet crew transmitted that they were experiencing brake issues and requested assistance from the FBO; including a tow.Contributing factors may have included limited situational awareness between aircraft operating in the traffic pattern and the inbound jet. The first transmission we heard from the jet was their 5-mile final call; which limited our awareness of their arrival and closure rate. Additionally; the use of only a tail number rather than a more descriptive aircraft identification made it more difficult to recognize the aircraft type and anticipate its higher approach speed.

column121: A potential near midair collision occurred while operating Aircraft X inbound to ZZZ from the northwest. The flight was returning early due to a student pilot not feeling well during the lesson.The aircraft was descending from 4;500 feet MSL to 3;500 feet MSL in preparation for passing beneath the ZZZ1 Class B airspace shelf. While monitoring ADS-B traffic; I observed another aircraft; Aircraft Y; southeast of our position and at a similar altitude. The aircraft appeared to be departing ZZZ2. At the time; we did not have the aircraft in visual sight.In an attempt to increase separation; I initiated a descent. However; it appeared on the traffic display that the other aircraft was also descending. Recognizing the potential conflict; I then initiated a climb. The other aircraft also appeared to begin climbing. During this maneuver; I acquired the aircraft visually and observed it at an estimated 300 to 500 feet of separation. The other aircraft initiated a left turn to avoid our aircraft; and I simultaneously executed a left turn to increase separation and avoid a collision.The conflict was resolved without further incident. The flight continued and terminated safely with no injuries or damage to either aircraft.At the time of the event; I was not in communication with ATC and was preparing to contact ZZZ Tower. I do not know whether the other aircraft was receiving ATC services or operating on the local practice area frequency.This event reinforced the importance of maintaining situational awareness; utilizing available traffic information; and remaining on the appropriate practice area frequency until ready to establish communication with the destination tower. Additionally; the event highlighted the importance of not assuming that another aircraft will maneuver in a predictable manner or based on perceived right-of-way considerations. Early visual acquisition and conservative avoidance actions remain critical to collision avoidance.

My first two transmissions received no response. On my third attempt; identifying myself as Aircraft X; the controller acknowledged my call sign. I advised the controller that a large jet had just passed directly over my aircraft near ZZZ with what appeared to be approximately 300 to 400 feet of vertical separation. The controller responded that he had not directed such traffic and advised me to contact ZZZ.

column121: On departure from runway XXL out of ZZZ I was PF and my Captain was PM. The takeoff roll and rotation occurred in sequence without any abnormalities. At positive rate I called for gear up and when the gear lever was moved into the up position I heard a loud crunching sound and then we got a cascade of EICAS massages including (LG LEVER DISAG; LG NOSE DOOR OPEN; AND LG WOW SYS FAIL). The EICAS also showed that the nose gear was in disagreement with the rest of the gear assembly. My captain notified departure of the situation and they put us on a heading and had us maintain 4000 feet as we sorted through the issue and ran the QRH. We ran the QRH in order of the messages that had appeared. The LG LEVER DISAG checklist led us to put the gear lever back in the down position- the actual action on the checklist says LANDING GEAR Lever- cycle; however once we put the gear down and were showing three green indications that the gear was down we decided to leave the lever in this position instead of retracting the gear again. Because the gear was all showing down this caused the LG LEVER DISAG message to go away. We then ran the checklist for the LG NOSE DOOR OPEN EICAS message and that specifically states to leave the gear lever down unless you need the performance to clear obstacles so this confirmed that our decision to leave the gear down was correct and then the LG WOW SYS FAIL directed us to land at the nearest suitable airport and it was at this point that we started setting up the ILS approach for XY. We were concerned that the nose wheel could be stuck in a position between fully down and fully up so we requested to do a low flyby over runway XY so that the tower could take a look and see if all three wheels appeared to be down. The tower said that everything looked normal so we came back around and shot a full flap approach to a landing as directed by the QRH. In my briefing I stated that I was going to keep as much back pressure on the airplane as I could so that the nose wheel came down gently in case it was not fully locked in the down position. Emergency vehicles looked at the aircraft upon exiting the runway and said that everything looked normal so we continued to taxi to the gate. On the post flight walk around I noticed that the outside of the nose wheels showed some of the metal had been sheared in some parts and that there was a noticeable puddle of hydraulic fluid that was actively leaking from the nose gear. The captain called maintenance and they were working on the issue when we left the plane.

column121: I was pilot flying as the captain on a short flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. I was unfamiliar with both airports due to being new to base. We saw before we had taken off that we were going to be close to landing weight; and we both noted it. Enroute; we received a runway change and experienced constant moderate chop; increasing workload and preventing us from increasing airspeed to burn more fuel; and I did not deploy spoilers early enough to be comfortably below landing weight on arrival. Upon beginning the visual approach to XXR; I started the descent late. I increased the Vertical Speed; and then turned my attention back to the fuel situation; deploying flaps 30; gear; and spoilers. When we were finished configuring; my FO noticed that we were about 400ft low at the final approach fix; receiving a Low Altitude Alert from ATC. As a result; we were close to 1000 ft HAT (Height Above Touchdown). I clicked off the autopilot; corrected to glide path; and called for flaps 45; but by the time flaps 45 had deployed we were around 800ft; and thus; unstable. I did not notice that we were unstable and we continued to land; which occurred uneventfullyCause: Unfamiliar airport as captain. Very short and compressed flight. Close to Landing weight limitation. Moderate turbulence. I was coming off of 3 weeks off.Suggestions: I could have deployed spoilers earlier to burn fuel faster and not had to worry about fuel as we got closer to ZZZ. Called Go Around when we saw that we were getting low at the FAF; and again when we were unstable at 1000ft. Asked ATC for delay vectors after the runway change.
column123: During a routine flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ we received a runway change from XYR to XXR. This is a short flight and as a result we were working quickly to switch the runways/obtain landing data/rebrief/etc. This led to task saturation in a busy environment during the arrival/approach phase of flight. We were also managing fuel as we were going to be close to max landing weight so the PF was trying to get flaps/gear/spoilers extended early to help increase our burn. As a result; we ended up starting our descent on the visual approach slightly late. The PF increased their descent rate to try and get back on a 3.0 degree glide. At this time we became distracted in making sure our landing weight was acceptable with the fuel on board. This led to us descending below a 3.0 glide; the PF noticed and disconnected the autopilot and began correcting the glide path. Shortly after we started correcting we received a low altitude warning from ATC. This occurred around ZZZZZ on the approach to XXR. The published altitude is 7;000' and we were around 6500'. At this point we were still flaps 30 so we began final configuration and the before landing check. We completed these tasks around 800' AGL and continued the approach and landing uneventfully.Cause: The cause of this event was task saturation combined with a distraction during a critical phase of flight that led to us not availing first. This resulted in getting low on a visual approach and not meeting the stabilized approach criteria at 1;000'. As PM I failed to call a go around at 1;000' and allowed the aircraft to continue. Another contributing factor was the short flight combined with a fuel load bringing us close to max landing weight. We attempted to burn fuel enroute with an increased speed but were not able to do so due to turbulence. Ultimately us fixating on the fuel during the final descent led to the deviation below glide path.Suggestions: Prior to the approach beginning we should have asked ATC for more time to get setup for the runway change to help manage our task saturation and mitigate rushing through those tasks. During the approach as PM I should have been more confident and assertive in calling the go around when we were low on the approach and unstable at 1'000 as we did not meet the stable approach criteria outlined in the Standard Operating Procedures for a visual approach.

column121: Today on flight to ZZZZ the crew and customers were put through extreme heat and dangerous conditions. Our concerns went unaddressed. The safety of crew and customers was compromised and ignored. All crew was at the gate for report time. We headed down to the plane. It was extremely hot. I told the agents. We proceeded to do our safety check and do a briefing. Maintenance came on and said the airplane should be cooling. It was not. I kept addressing this and my concerns were brushed off. Operations said the plane would cool down also. The pilots finally got onboard about 10 minutes prior to boarding and were able to start cooling down the plane. We decided it was okay to proceed with an on time boarding as the aircraft (AC) was getting much cooler. About 10 minutes into boarding the AC got unbearably hot again. I got stuck for a little while trying to make my way up the aisle (I was doing pre-departure beverages) then finally got to the flight deck.They said the APU broke and we never should have boarded. Nobody ever told me this and we were almost done boarding.Operations wanted to deplane all customers; the pilots did not. The pilots told the agents to get everyone on as quickly as possible so we could close the door and start an engine and the plane would begin to cool. I informed my crew and made a PA. At this point people were complaining nonstop. We had two kids in the back not feeling well and had bright red faces. A mother of an infant onboard removed all of the baby's clothing as she feared the infant was overheating. One FA in the back was dripping with sweat. Another FA in the back had to sit down for a couple minutes as he began to feel faint. Several customers started asking for water. I started feeling very nauseous. We got everyone on and seated and very quickly closed the overhead bins. Due to this pressure to board so quickly; FA A hurt his bag rushing to assist a customer who was dropping a bag. We made him an ice pack for his back and I checked on him throughout the flight. Nonetheless; we got all bins closed within about two minutes per the captain and were ready to close. Then we had to wait on AFT catering; then we had to wait on Maintenance. I kept being told; 'a couple more minutes' which in reality was about 10-15 minutes. It was pure chaos and misery. I kept being told different things by different people. People kept telling us it would cool down. One person; even said the plane would cool when the cabin door was shut. We shut the door hoping to finally have some relief. This was the opposite of the truth. It just kept getting hotter. The pilots said we couldn't start the engine yet due to Maintenance. Every concern I had just kept getting completely brushed off and ignored. It was so dangerous and my crew and I genuinely felt helpless. I didn't even know what to keep telling the customers as it was NOT getting cooler. We finally pushed back and it was still so hot. The pilots said it was around 85° in the cabin. We did the safety video and our compliance checks. The engine was started so we were told it would cool; but then the captain said it wouldn't cool until we got into the air. It was still hot during flight; the pilots said their gauge read around 77° but would continue to go down. About one hour into the flight the temperature had gotten to 79°. The captain said the middle of the cabin has to cool before the rest of the plane cools.We kept being assured the plane would cool but several different people throughout this entire experience. The plane did not get cooler until about 3 hours into the flight. I don't understand why we were strung along. I felt so bad making PA's telling the customers the plane would cool; when in reality nothing was happening. There were so many excuses as to why the plane was so hot. No crew or customers should ever have to go through this. It creates a hazardous environment and I wish our concerns had been addressed instead of brushed off.

column121: We arrived at ZZZ from ZZZ1; returning from a family vacation. We needed to drop one passenger off at ZZZ . The arrival and landing into ZZZ were uneventful; including a long taxi from XXR to the FBO with zero issues. After adding 20 gallons of fuel and using the bathrooms; we did a quick check of the plane and boarded our final leg to Location X. We had also performed thorough preflight checks in ZZZ1 before the first flight of the day and found zero issues. We picked up our IFR clearance and taxied out behind a TBM also departing runway XY. After a quick run-up holding short; we were cleared to depart XY. Entering the runway; applied take off power; verified instruments in the green; called out airspeed alive everything was normal; and right at 50kts or so; the plane almost instantly veered to the left; and we began hearing 'thuds' similar to a flat tire; so did what had to be done to keep us on the runway and was able to do so even though it was a wild ride for a moment Unfortunately; we came to rest at an intersection between XY and XXR; which caused a delay in airport ops. The FBO; originally tried to come tug us to the shop within 10min of being there but with the tire blown it wasn't happening. The jack they originally brought to raise the gear got jammed and was not able to move it for a good 20min. The fire department was called out to help lift the plane off the original jack; which took some time and all of us were working to move as quickly as possible. Then a local MX (Maintenance) shop arrived with larger jacks; and their jack also jammed (fun times); and they broke a few smaller skid plates attempting to move the plane back to the MX shop of their own property. They finally used a forklift under the gear and towed the plane back slowly to the shop.  We are grateful they were able to get it; as an airport ops manager told one of the people assisting us if it wasn't moved quickly; they 'would come drag it off with city services'. The local airport ops who were assisting us; and the fire department; the FBO; and MX shop all really did their best. WE ALL DID. column121: While in steady state cruise with the autopilot engaged at 8500' MSL we heard a 'bang'. In addition; the ignition monitoring device showed no issues with the ignition.Next was to initiate a 180-degree turn to the left; back towards ZZZ; which we had just passed; and requested priority handling with ZZZ Approach. The 'High Aspect' ratio wing of the RV-9; with full flaps; a full deflection slip; and a little bit of power from the engine; had me descending at around 650 FPM at 75 knots IAS; which is 15 knots faster than normal. A broken valve stem from cylinder #2 migrated into the carburetor and would not allow me to close the throttle fully. The residual power from the function two cylinders produced enough thrust to significantly extend my glide.I touched down past mid-field and had enough energy to coast to a taxiway and exit the runway; where the engine stopped running without input from me.Upon initial inspection; the exhaust valve stem from cylinder #2 failed and migrated through the engine. Part of the valve damaged cylinder #1 and pounded close the sparkplugs; so that cylinder was not making power; but had some compression.Cylinder #2 was making no compression.A part of the #2 exhaust valve cassed through the carburetor was found in the filtered airbox. The valve stem from the exhaust valve was found the throat of the carburetor and prevented the throttle to close. The throttle could only move from full open to half open; it could not be closed.This resulted in me not being able to close the throttle fully and what power the engine could make; significantly increased my glide distance.Based on the data from the avionics; it was exactly eight minutes from engine failure to touchdown. During the eight-minute glide the engine continued to vibrate violently; produce loud backfires in the exhaust; and as we found out from the people on the ground; trailing black smoke.

column121: I am a recently instrument-rated private pilot with approximately 450 total flight hours operating a turbocharged Piper PA-32 single-engine piston aircraft not approved for flight into known icing. I departed ZZZ1 VFR with flight following; returning to ZZZ; a non-towered airport.Afternoon convective activity was present. Prior to departure; I completed a weather briefing and planned a route north of the convective activity with the intent to cross in an area that appeared less active before turning south toward ZZZ.After departure; I proceeded northwestbound and cleared the ZZZ1 Class B. Based on visual observations and available weather information at the time; conditions appeared to permit a crossing while remaining clear of cloud; and I requested an IFR pop-up clearance to cross the ridge. ZZZ Center approved the clearance. I climbed in orbits to FL240 and was subsequently cleared direct to my destination.While proceeding westbound; it became apparent that convective build-ups were developing along my route. I received ATC approval for multiple heading deviations; including a larger left deviation; to remain clear of weather. As I approached the ridge at FL240; the visual corridor between cloud formations narrowed and I no longer observed a clear path forward that would allow me to remain clear of clouds.At that point; I decided to request to reverse course toward Area X and made two radio calls requesting a turn-back and vectors. Neither transmission was acknowledged. After the unanswered calls; I became concerned that communications may not have been effective and was preparing to squawk 7600.At approximately the same time; while near the ridge at FL240; I encountered a significant downdraft and became unable to maintain assigned altitude. The aircraft began a rapid descent. I lowered the nose to maintain airspeed and made a small heading adjustment to remain clear of a nearby convective build-up.During this descent; ZZZ Center transmitted instructions to maintain FL240 due to traffic behind and below me on a similar route of flight. I responded 'unable.' ATC subsequently issued traffic avoidance instructions to the trailing aircraft. Based on ADS-B In observations; closest proximity appeared to remain approximately 5 to 6 miles laterally with vertical separation maintained.I continued the descent through a visual opening into VMC; remained in communication with ATC; cancelled IFR descending through 18;000 feet; and proceeded to an uneventful landing at ZZZ1. No injury; aircraft damage; or loss of control occurred.Contributing factors included afternoon convective activity over high terrain; acceptance of direct routing rather than continuation of my original planned route north of the weather; operation at high altitude with aircraft performance considerations; the need to remain clear of cloud due to icing concerns; and a period in which my radio transmissions requesting a turn-back were not acknowledged by ATC.Lessons learned from this event for me include maintaining more conservative margins for mountain crossings in convective conditions; adhering to pre-planned routing around weather rather than accepting more direct options when conditions are deteriorating; and communicating changing circumstances to ATC earlier when weather avoidance or aircraft performance begins limiting available options. I have debriefed this flight in detail with experienced CFIIs and mentors and am incorporating these lessons into future weather assessment; route selection; and mountain flying decision making.
