column121: My student and I conducted a Commercial Multi-Engine training flight. Before departure; a thorough preflight inspection was completed in accordance with the aircraft checklist and company procedures. Particular attention was given to the landing gear system; including the actuators; bolts; J-hooks; springs; switches; and all visible components. No discrepancies or abnormalities were observed. Following engine start; we taxied to the Run-up pad of Runway XXR at ZZZ1. A normal run-up was completed per checklist; and all aircraft systems operated within normal parameters. We departed and proceeded southwest; climbing to between 4;500 and 4;700 feet MSL. During the flight; we performed several training maneuvers; including an accelerated stall; a VMC demonstration; and an emergency descent. During the emergency descent; the landing gear was extended (below VLO) and indicated normal operation: three green gear lights were illuminated; no gear-unsafe indication was present; and the nose gear appeared down and locked when visually checked in the mirror. We recovered from the maneuver at approximately 2;500 feet MSL and continued a gradual descent to 2;000 feet MSL. I then instructed the student to don a view-limiting device for instrument training; and we conducted a simulated RNAV Runway XYR approach into ZZZ. A simulated left-engine failure was introduced; and the student completed the required procedures in accordance with the checklist standard operating procedures. We received the ATIS at ZZZ and proceeded to contact ZZZ Tower (Approximately 13 NM west of the airport) and were instructed to enter left traffic for Runway XZ. The approach was discontinued at approximately 1;000 feet MSL to establish proper spacing in the traffic pattern. Abeam the 1;000-foot markers on the downwind leg for Runway XZ; the landing gear was extended. All indications appeared normal; including three green gear lights; no red gear-unsafe indication; and visual confirmation of the nose gear position in the mirror. Flaps were extended to 10° to slow the aircraft to approximately 100 MPH; followed by 25° once landing was assured. At approximately 500 feet AGL; the standard landing checklist and callouts were completed: fuel selectors ON; mixtures FULL RICH; propellers FULL FORWARD; landing gear DOWN (three green; no red; and one visible in the mirror); fuel pumps ON; and landing lights ON. Final approach speed was approximately 87 MPH in accordance with company operating procedures. The aircraft touched down smoothly on the runway centerline without incident and the landing gear initially supported the aircraft normally. Because this was a touch-and-go landing; the student retracted the flaps and applied takeoff power. During the transition to the go portion of the maneuver; the nose landing gear suddenly collapsed. The student immediately closed both throttles; and I immediately moved both mixture controls to cutoff. I assumed control of the aircraft and elected not to apply brakes or rudder inputs to avoid aggravating the situation. The aircraft veered approximately 10-15 feet left of the runway centerline and came to rest between Taxiways 1 and 2. I informed the tower that we had experienced a nose gear collapse; and the tower advised that airport rescue and firefighting personnel were responding. After the aircraft came to a complete stop; I secured the aircraft by turning off both magnetos; electric fuel pumps; lights; alternators; and the master switch. I then instructed the student to follow my lead during the evacuation; and we exited the aircraft and moved to a safe location aft of the right wing. Approximately one hour later; the Chief Flight Instructor; Assistant Chief Flight Instructor; and maintenance personnel arrived from ZZZ1. The aircraft was lifted and towed to a parking area at ZZZ. After the aircraft was secured; the head of maintenance advised that the cause of the incident was not yet known and that the left main landing gear had apparently not fully locked; although it had supported the aircraft during the landing rollout. The aircraft remained supported by its landing gear and was parked at ZZZ. I proceeded to speak to my assistant chief flight instructor and he said something along the lines of 'they knew it was going to happen at some point' or 'It was inevitable' and that he was glad that it did not happen to him (he was the pilot that flew the aircraft before I did).For context; similar nose gear collapse events have occurred previously within our PA-34-200 fleet; including at least one involving this same aircraft. A known limitation during preflight inspection is the plastic fairing beneath the nose gear; which restricts visibility of several components of the nose gear assembly. Improved inspection access either by removing the fairing during inspection or redesigning it to permit better visual access may help identify potential discrepancies before flight.
column123: I met with my instructor to conduct a commercial multi-engine training flight. Prior to departure; we completed a thorough preflight inspection of the aircraft in accordance with the checklist and company procedures. No discrepancies or abnormalities were observed.After engine start; we taxied to the run-up area and completed all required engine and systems checks. Everything operated normally; and there were no indications of any mechanical issues. We then departed from Runway XXR at ZZZ1 and proceeded southwest of the airspace to conduct training maneuvers. During the flight; we practiced accelerated stalls; simulated engine failures; VMC demonstrations; and emergency descent procedures.Following completion of the maneuvers; my instructor assumed control and had me wear a view-limiting device to simulate an instrument approach with an engine failure scenario. We flew toward ZZZ and conducted the RNAV Runway XYR approach. Air traffic control subsequently instructed us to enter a left downwind for Runway XZ. My instructor directed me to continue the approach visually; and I removed the view-limiting device. While entering the traffic pattern; we completed the before-landing checklist multiple times. I verified that the landing gear was extended and indicating down; and my instructor independently verified the gear position as well. The approach was stable; and we made a normal landing on the centerline of Runway XZ.After touchdown; we initiated a touch-and-go. Once clear of the landing roll; I retracted the flaps in accordance with procedure and smoothly applied takeoff power. Shortly thereafter; the nose of the aircraft suddenly collapsed onto the runway. I immediately retarded the throttles to idle. My instructor took control of the aircraft; secured both engines by bringing the mixtures to idle cutoff; and completed the appropriate shutdown procedures. We remained in the aircraft until it came to a complete stop. After coordinating with the control tower; we exited the aircraft safely without injury.At no point during the flight; approach; or landing did I observe any indication that the landing gear system was malfunctioning. The landing itself was normal; and the nose gear collapse occurred during the attempted touch-and-go after power had been applied for takeoff.

column121: When I got the Flight Plan (release 1) from dispatch I took the time to review as I typically do...including the maintenance write-ups. I noticed an inbound pilot defect report indicating the #2 pack overheated and that it was a repeat write-up. I also noticed a deferral for an inop zone hot air pressure regulating valve.  Zone ducts temps were over 80 and A/C zones very hot. Temp was regulated by closing hot air regulating valve...and this was on deferral. Additionally; there were a few previous write-ups on pack #2 overheating. There was also a previous Unable-to-operate for pack 1 and 2 faults. During this review process I got input from my FO who has lots of experience on the airbus. We talked about potential threats and what we could do to mitigate. However; those conversations were based on pack #2 actually being fixed after the initial overheat. That said; we knew of the inbound pilot defect report and the issue with pack #2 repeating. After speaking with the inbound Captain about his defect report and how he handled the issue (he was told the pack was fixed but obviously the issue had not been resolved); I seriously questioned whether or not I was going to accept the aircraft. At this point I had enough data points to question the safe operation of the aircraft. So I decided to call Maintenance Control and discuss the pack issues. Maintenance Control told me they had issue with pack 1 a few times before they were to get it fixed and that they were pretty sure it was now a good pack. I didnt get the sense the fix on pack 1 was an absolute; especially with the repeat write-ups and issues with pack 2; as well as the previous unable to operate due to both packs faulting. To add to it; there was significant weather in ZZZ for our departure time (while at the gate we experienced light hail; heavy rain; lightning; and I was told a tornado warning). All factors considered I was leaning toward refusing the aircraft. At about that time I spoke with a ZZZ Maintenance (MX) tech who came out to the aircraft to collect a readout from the aircraft regarding the packs and associated failures. He told me that his supervisor was considering removing the aircraft from service due to the pack issues and their history. However; MX eventually decided to defer the #2 pack under MEL XXXXX. This would basically put us on single pack operations; and any issues with pack one would result in an emergency descent. It was at that time I decided to refuse the aircraft. Based on the history of previous issues with both packs; and #2 pack overheating multiple times after repairs; I did not feel safe operating this aircraft. To add to the confusion; while the pack deferral was pushed through and approved; the release was still red for an inop windshield wiper that could not be fixed due to the ramp being closed for lightning. I was getting pressured by ZZZ Operations to board the aircraft; but I told them it wasn't a good idea because I was going to refuse the aircraft. So I decided to call Maintenance Control to see if he could help start the refusal process; which he did. I wanted the system to show the refusal so Operations would be able to move forward and stop trying to board passengers. I then called dispatch to inform them and he also entered the refusal into the system.  After that; things settled down and we received a new aircraft...I was coming in about an hour and half later.

column121: We departed ZZZZ; en route to ZZZ. I was the Pilot Flying (PF); and the Captain was performing Pilot Monitoring (PM) duties.The takeoff was normal; and the aircraft became airborne without any abnormalities. Shortly after gear retraction; a Master Caution illuminated along with a hydraulic indication. The Captain advised that we had an Engine No. 1 HYD PUMP LOW PRESSURE indication.We continued the departure; accelerated as planned; selected Flaps 1 and then Flaps Up; and completed the After Takeoff Checklist. I requested that the Captain accomplish the applicable Engine No. 1 HYD PUMP LOW PRESSURE checklist. At that time; Hydraulic System A quantity was indicating approximately 15%; with only the Engine No. 1 HYD PUMP LOW PRESSURE light illuminated. The associated checklist was completed; and no additional immediate actions were required.The Captain advised ATC of the situation and requested to maintain 7;000 feet while entering a holding pattern at ZZZZZ to evaluate the condition. During the hold; the applicable non-normal checklist was completed. The Captain coordinated with Dispatch; communicated with ATC; and informed the cabin crew and passengers.After all applicable non-normal checklists had been completed and all required actions had been accomplished; I transferred aircraft control to the Captain to facilitate the approach briefing and arrival preparation. During the briefing; we brief the weather; landing performance; overweight landing considerations; threat assessment; and return options. We determined that returning to ZZZZ was the safest course of action. The decision and operational plan were communicated to Dispatch; ATC; the cabin crew; and the passengers.Landing performance data was obtained and reviewed. We selected MAX AUTOBRAKE and planned a Flaps 40 landing. The approach briefing was completed; inbound course and minimums were set; and all required preparations were accomplished. I then resumed Pilot Flying duties and requested the Descent Checklist.After verifying that all required actions had been completed; we requested the approach. ATC cleared us direct ZZZZZ1; instructed us to descend and maintain 4;000 feet; and subsequently cleared us for the approach. I requested that the Captain verify and set a re-cruise altitude of 4;000 feet in the FMC to ensure VNAV guidance remained available during the approach.The approach was flown normally. While established on final; I requested Flaps 30 and subsequently Flaps 40. Shortly after Flaps 40 extension; we observed Hydraulic System A quantity decrease to zero. At that time; we were approximately 1;000-1;100 feet AGL. The landing gear was down; flaps were fully extended; and the aircraft remained stabilized on approach. Given the aircraft configuration and compliance with stabilized approach criteria; we elected to continue.Prior to landing; the Captain reminded me that with the loss of Hydraulic System A; reverse thrust availability and braking characteristics could be affected and that accumulator performance should be monitored. I acknowledged the briefing.I disconnected the autopilot and landed the aircraft normally. Only the No. 2 (right) thrust reverser was utilized. Braking performance was normal; and we exited the runway at Taxiway 1.After clearing the runway; I completed the After Landing Flow and started the APU. While reviewing the Hydraulic System A Loss checklist; we reached a step directing us to select Nose Wheel Steering Alternate. After selecting the alternate mode; taxi capability improved; however; we then observed Hydraulic System B quantity beginning to decrease as well.Recognizing the potential for further degradation of aircraft systems; the Captain elected to stop the aircraft and set the parking brake. We advised ATC that we were unable to continue taxiing under our own power. Hydraulic System B quantity continued to decrease. The APU was placed on the bus; and we continued coordinating with ATC; the cabin crew; passengers;and company personnel.I contacted the company and advised that a tow would be required because we could no longer safely taxi the aircraft due to the continued loss of hydraulic fluid. Maintenance; Dispatch; Scheduling; and the Chief Pilot were notified.A tow vehicle arrived and towed the aircraft to Gate XX without further incident. The passengers remained informed throughout the event. After arrival at the gate; passengers deplaned normally; and Maintenance assumed control of the aircraft for further evaluation.No injuries occurred; and the event was managed in accordance with SOPs; company procedures; and non-normal checklist guidance.We were approximately 1;400 pounds above the maximum landing weight.

column121: Just before the top of descent on the OBRUG1B; we noticed a GPS-L INVALID on the Control Display Unit (CDU) scratchpad. We referred to the Flight Manual (FM) and since we had briefed the RNP 22 approach; we wanted to check the requirements for that approach. The NAV STATUS page showed GPS (2) and we were satisfied that we could continue with the RNP approach.Mazatlan Control gave us a clearance to cross MURES at FL230; which we programmed into the FMC. We also kept OBRUG at FL 230; since we were cleared to descend via the OBRUG1B to 5500'.At the top of descent; we descended in VNAV and crossed MURES at FL230; but the aircraft continued to descend (about 250 ft) below FL 230; even though we were supposed to remain at FL 230  until descending again at OBRUG. Autopilot A was engaged. I engaged vertical speed to gradually climb the aircraft back to FL230; then re-engaged VNAV (this was about 16 nm prior to OBRUG). The aircraft started to descend again; so I intervened again to stop the descent. At OBRUG; I re-engaged VNAV; and the aircraft remained at or above the path throughout the remainder of the arrival and approach (RNP 22). We were monitoring it closely; of course.On short final; the FO (pilot monitoring) observed a GPS-L INVALID message; followed by a GPS-R INVALID message on the CDU scratchpad.The conditions were VMC and I was hand flying from about 1000 feet. We landed normally and taxied to the gate; then completed two Electronic Log Book write-ups (one about the VNAV issue and one about the GPS INVALID messages).I contacted dispatch; who connected me with Maintenance Control; and we notified the local station about the write-ups. A mechanic came on board shortly; and spoke to us; as well as Maintenance Control. The local mechanic said that the GPS issue was likely related to signal blocking. I don't know whether this is true or not; but he seemed pretty certain that this was likely the case.On a recent flight (a couple of weeks ago) going into PVR; I recall getting the GPS-L INVALID message; but it cleared on its own after a few minutes.There weren't any NOTAMS related to GPS signal issues on our flight. This seems to be a recurring issue that probably should be put out there to the pilot group (NOTAM or bulletin of some sort) so that crews can be aware of this potential issue and plan accordingly.

column121: During approach ILS XX ZZZ. Inclement weather approaching the final course caused winds to vary widely in both speed and direction. Upon initiation of approach through to beyond final approach course approach was stabilized despite significantly variable winds. At some point slightly beyond final approach fix aircraft began sinking below ILS glideslope and glide slope aural warning was heard. Corrective action taken immediately. One dot low glideslope indication noticed. Runway was in sight at this time 3 red PAPIs indicated. Ground Proximity switch light illuminated briefly while corrections were being applied. 'Terrain terrain' aural annunciation not heard. Glide path was corrected and approach continued no go around initiated.Cause: Variable winds caused by approaching inclement weather made for a difficult approach. Pilots decision to attempt the approach despite approaching weatherSuggestions: Pilots should have elected to hold and wait out the weather. More assertive corrective actions would have decreased the mount of time spent in deviation from glideslope.
column123: During turn to intercept final approach course on ILS XX ZZZ flaps 20 were selected. Speed was under control during the initiation of the turn but as the localizer course became alive winds shifted due to weather entering the area. Airspeed (210 selected and indicated and initiation of the turn) increased significantly and caused an overspeed of approximately 3-5 knots at flaps 20. The event was noticed and autopilot disconnected and corrections initiated immediately but not sufficient to overcome the changing winds. Overspeed clacker sounded momentarily. Power was reduced significantly and pitch angle increased to reduce airspeed. Airspeed was in the red for approximately 5-10 seconds.Cause: Increased indicated airspeed due to approaching weather and failure to react in sufficient time and assertiveness.Suggestions: The event could have been avoided entirely if pilots had elected to hold and wait out the weather. A larger difference between selected airspeed and maximum airspeed could have given pilots more time to react. (IE 200 selected at flaps 20 rather than 210)

column121: This was the third 20 minute ride flight of the day out of seven scheduled.  The first two flights were uneventful.  On the third flight while landing on runway XX at ZZZ; the winds were reported to be 260 degrees at 12 gust to 18 knots.  During the flare for the three point landing; the wind abruptly shifted to 330 degrees at 15 gust to 23 knots; as reported by the Tower after the incident.  I immediately put in additional crosswind controls to prevent the airplane from being affected by the unforeseen wind shift; but it was too late.  The airplane was already starting to weathervane and started to ground loop.  I stayed on the surface of the runway and then began to swerve onto taxiway 'H' to the north of the runway.  After stopping on the taxiway; facing opposite the landing direction; I radioed to the Tower 'We're good.'  I never left the prepared surface; nor did I contact the left wing with the ground.  A brief conversation with the Tower Controller also said that he was caught by surprise with the sudden wind shift as well and he was surprised how well I had handled the situation.  He also said that after the wind shift he was changing the landing runway from runway XX to runway XY.  I taxied the airplane to its parking location and did a thorough post flight inspection for any possible damage to the aircraft wings and landing gear; of which there was none.

column121: On the date of Day 0 I conducted an IFR flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. On my route I was cleared for a Direct as filed at 8;000'. At approximately 1.5 hours into my flight I received an carbon monoxide warning on my foreflight app which was detected by the carbon monoxide detector in my sentry ADSB receiver. Immediately following this message I equipped my nasal oxygen cannula and ensured my oxygen flow was set via my oxygen delivery system. Once my cannula was mounted properly and my oxygen was flowing I contacted ATC and let them know of the warning and that I was on oxygen and not feeling any symptoms. Due to my position and lack of apparent symptoms I decided to continue to my original destination airport ZZZ. In my flight bag I have a blood oxygen monitor that my company requires me to bring with me on all my flights due to the high altitude we do our single pilot aerial surveys at; but I unfortunately placed my flight bag entirely out of reach on this flight due to the fact that I knew I would be flying at a low altitude because I was ferrying the aircraft. Being in and out of IMC at night I decided to focus entirely on flying the plane and recognizing any symptoms that I may be encountering due to the levels of carbon monoxide detected in the cabin instead of trying to find my blood oxygen sensor. after about 15-20 more minutes into the flight and receiving clearance to descend and then to follow a 737 into ZZZ for a visual approach I had a much harder time finding the airport than I normally would; everything below 8;000' was entirely clear and it being at night a larger airport like ZZZ should not be this hard to find. After finally finding the airport and getting clearance to land about 5-7 miles out; I ran my checklist 3 or 4 extra times to ensure myself not to miss any important pre landing checklist items. At this time I was feeling light headed but was very focused on landing my airplane and making mental notes to worry about dealing with that task before self diagnosing any symptoms I may be feeling from the situation. Once I landed and had a rather smooth landing considering the circumstances I remember being told to turn right off the runway and I believe being asked where I was planning on parking. When I finally stopped moving and was clear of the active runway I remember feeling a wave of light headedness; a slight to moderate headache and a dry mouth. I remember tower reading my taxi clearance to me and was hit with what I can only describe as a wave of confusion as I was not only able to read the taxi clearance back properly but also truly couldn't put it to practice in my head. Something as simple as a taxi clearance is muscle memory to me at this point in my career so I instantly knew something was definitely wrong. So I immediately opened the door and window and told tower/ground that I was experiencing carbon monoxide poisoning symptoms. I remember ground telling me I could shut off my aircraft where I was and after turning off my avionics it took me a solid 60 seconds to remember the exact process of shutting down my aircraft. After this I remember setting the parking brake and getting out of the aircraft and feeling quite light headed and my legs were weak. An airport ops manager drove up to me and offered me to sit down in his car and gave me water and I sat with him until the medics arrived. At this point I had probably been on the ground and out of the aircraft for about 12 minutes; the confusion began to fade rather quickly but the light headedness remained until the end of the evening slight fatigue and 'brain fog' persisted for the following 24ish hours following the event. The medics implemented a few tests on me and if I remember correctly they said my blood sugar/blood pressure was entirely normal range but there was another test which I think was related to CO poisoning that they said was rather high but not of a hospitalization level. After this the medics cleared me to go and I and the airportops manager received clearance for him to escort me and my taxi to the ramp.

column121: During a multiengine commercial pilot training flight; a simulated engine failure was introduced during the takeoff roll prior to rotation (VR). Although the procedure was briefly discussed during taxi; the lack of previous practical introduction to this maneuver and single-engine muscle memory led to delayed throttle reduction; causing a loss of directional control and a runway excursion. No damage or injuries occurred.I was performing a training flight in a Piper Seminole (PA-44) to prepare for my upcoming Commercial Multiengine checkride. I had already completed some prior training sessions in the aircraft type. This specific emergency maneuver had never been practiced in my previous flights; and it was not included in our pre-flight briefing. After our third landing at ZZZ Airport; the flight instructor requested to taxi back to active Runway XX for another takeoff. During the taxi; the instructor briefed me that we would perform an engine failure during the takeoff roll. He asked me to recite the correct procedure; and I correctly stated the steps: throttles to idle; apply full braking; and maintain directional control on the runway. However; during the actual takeoff roll; prior to reaching rotation speed (VR); the instructor simulated the engine failure. Despite having just discussed the procedure; my lack of practical experience with this maneuver and entrenched single-engine muscle memory caused me to freeze on the throttles. Instead of immediately retarding them to IDLE; I attempted to maintain the centerline using rudder inputs alone. Before VR; the rudder lacked the aerodynamic authority to counteract the severe asymmetric thrust of the operating engine at full takeoff power. The aircraft veered off the centerline; resulting in a low-speed runway excursion into the grass adjacent to Runway XX.The instructor took control; power was reduced to idle; and the aircraft was safely stopped and secured. A thorough inspection confirmed there was no damage to the aircraft; no damage to airport property; and no injuries to either occupant. The checkride scheduled was canceled.This event highlighted a major disconnect between theoretical knowledge and practical muscle memory during high-workload multiengine emergencies. Even though I knew the procedure and recited it minutes prior; the lack of previous physical repetition caused a failure in execution. Moving forward; I am committing to intensive 'chair flying' and dedicated dual training to mechanize the immediate physical reaction of bringing throttles to IDLE during an aborted takeoff before rescheduling my checkride.

column121: I was working the ZZZZZ position; frequency 120.45; with a string of arrivals inbound to IAD on the GIBBZ5 Arrival. It was a bit of an unusual sequence due to weather near IAD. Airplanes on the north leg of the arrival were being vectored off the arrival and given to the ZZZZZ1 / ZZZZZ2 sector for Runway 19L and the south leg of the arrival I was vectoring to a right base leg to Runway 19C. Aircraft X checked in on the north leg and I instructed them to descend to 070. I then went to issue a turn to Aircraft Y to the base leg and got no response. I tried the turn again; no response. I reached out to two other aircraft with no response. I changed my transmitter to standby and tried again with no response. I plugged into the Emergency Communication System (ECS) orange box and tried that and still got no response. All of a sudden; I had lost any way of communicating with any of the aircraft I was talking to and they were all on vectors. My last chance was to plug back into the RDVS (Rapid Deployment Voice Switch) and attempt the tunable frequency which finally worked. However; due to the delay in communication; two aircraft had left my frequency (one to guard and one to a different approach sector). So now I was scrambling to keep aircraft separated and sequenced with a very limited capacity to talk to any of them; as well as coordinate with the other sectors who had gotten aircraft they weren't expecting. It made an already complicated session exponentially more difficult and affected the flow of traffic to the airport.Recommendation: There needs to be more reliable equipment to start with; but certainly a wider array of backup options. For me to be working and have aircraft on headings to lose everything was a very disconcerting experience. It's almost daily that there are frequencies that are out of service or being worked on so there is no backup. And often; when they are returned to service; the quality isn't great. Coverage is less than ideal. Even when the actual frequency came back; I reached out to a pilot and they said they were only receiving me 3x5.

column121: Aircraft X was flashing at me from the ZZZ ARTCC sector XX. The aircraft altitude was showing 030B040 and in the 4th line he was deviating left and direct ZZZ when able. The ZZZ [ARTCC] controller called me on the landline and apreq'd (Approval Request) the aircraft in the block. I advised the controller that at 030 I would most likely not be able to communicate with the a/c (Aircraft) throughout my airspace. The ZZZ [ARTCC] controller told the pilot that and said that he was requesting the block for weather and suggested that he amend the block to 030B050 so he can climb higher for communications; which I approved. Also the ZZZ [ARTCC] controller requested ZZZ approaches frequency as a backup for the aircraft; which I gave him XXX.XX.As the a/c entered my airspace; he continued to deviate for weather. As he deviated an MSAW alert started on the aircraft. I then realized he was deviating into an MEA of 3200 ft. and was level at 3000 ft. I immediately attempted to give the aircraft a low altitude alert warning with no response. I then attempted to contact the a/c on the guard frequency; also with no response. Following that I contacted Aircraft Y to relay on XXX.XY (the west frequency of Sector XY). Aircraft Y tried multiple times with no response. I also attempted contact again with my BUEC (Backup Emergency Communications) transmitters with no response. With this unfortunate turn of events Aircraft X traversed the 3200 MEA without incident. However; there was another 3200 ft. MEA coming up. I advised the Supervisor of the situation and told them the steps I had been taking.I called the ZZZ approach controller to see if he could reach out on XXX.XX and see if Aircraft X was monitoring. The ZZZ [TRACON] controller advised that the pilot was not answering. I then called the ZZZ [ARTCC] controller to see if he could reach out to the aircraft and see if he was still on his frequency. The controller called and said he was not on frequency. I queried what frequency the ZZZ [ARTCC] controller transferred him to; and he told me that he told the a/c to monitor XXX.XZ (the east frequency for Sector XY). Due to this new information I adjusted my attempts and contacted Aircraft Z and asked him to relay on XXX.XZ. Aircraft Z was able to reach Aircraft X on the first call; and I asked Aircraft Z to climb him immediately to 3200 ft.; which Aircraft X confirmed and enacted. I then asked Aircraft Z to amend his block altitude to 032B050 which also was accomplished. Eventually I was able to reach Aircraft X on XXX.XZ as he got closer to the transmitter and establish communications. After I Apreq'd the new block altitude and deviations to the ZZZ approach controller I transferred communications to the ZZZ approach controller. The a/c continued his flight without incident.I think this situation could have been prevented if I would have insisted on climbing the aircraft to 4000 ft. The weather was already providing an unknown to the aircrafts route of flight and the communication barrier made it so it would have been the best proactive response. However I allowed it because the a/c requested the block for weather purposes. One thing that would have also prevented this would have been if the ZZZ [ARTCC] controller would have transferred communications to the correct (west) frequency. This confusion made me take several actions that were counterproductive to fixing the situation. Had I known he was on the East frequency; I believe Aircraft Y would have reached Aircraft X the first time and avoided the MEA.

column121: We were told by tech ops to go to ES (Emergency Service) mode for a system update that sometimes happens on Day 0 night mids. The scope next to me was still up so I was able to use that for reference. In the past when a scope goes black; we usually are told to go to ES; but tonight they were working the FS (Full Service) mode so I am unsure of going to another mode would have worked. We yelled over at tech ops and the OMIC (Operations Manager in Charge) about our scopes. They acknowledged but didn't come over to offer help. Tech ops seemed to be working on the issue in the middle area and for a brief time every scope went black for a few seconds before they all came back on. Last week during the middle of the day; the Sunol scope went completely blank. Last week night mid; SFO tower scopes went black and multiple go arounds ensued with chaos at the Area B mid sector. Had the Area B controller agreed to switch to ES earlier tonight (they asked twice); it would have been terrible from a safety standpoint. Why is this stuff happening now? column121: I operated flight ABCD ZZZ1 to ZZZ with my FO. We were late blocking out of ZZZ1 because the server went down and we ultimately had to leave 9 people behind because dispatch didn't want to delay the flight anymore. We had a MEL that required us to start the #2 engine at the gate because the cross bleed valve was broken so the apu or the #1 engine couldn't assist with the start. Pretty uneventful taxi out of ZZZ1 we were taking off XYL tower told us there was no EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time) time for us which I found very odd because I looked and saw we had a XA:03 edct we quiwered tower and they said they just got off the phone with center and there was no hold for release. I was pilot monitoring and FO was pilot flying to ZZZ. The take off and climb were pretty uneventful. Once we got to ZZZZZ on the arrival atc started telling every plane behind us that they will be holding or they need to divert for the weather. I asked ATC and they said we will be the last plane to land in ZZZ before they close the field we got set up and reviewed for the ILS XXC with the winds it was a gust factor of plus 14 on the speeds we talked about the weather and the threats and the possibility of Windshear and rain on final. We both had our radars up monitoring the storm and ATC was telling us that the storm had not reached the field yet it was a couple miles away and everybody was still getting in. We got vectored off the star and put on a long straight in final for XXC I asked FO if we was comfortable landing giving the weather and if we wanted me to he said he was good he would fly it. Everybody was getting in fine infront of us a little further on the approach tower said they were not reporting some windshear and a gain of 20 knots that's when I asked FO again if he was comfortable even with the wind shear. We got cleared for the approach and He elected for me to land the plane so we swapped controls. the planes in front of us landing never had windshear. We were 4 miles behind another 175 and they got in no problem at about 1000 feet I kicked off the auto pilot and hand flew the airplane and at about 800 feet we got a massive push of air that threw us up a couple hundred feet and increased our speed 15 knots we were not stable I called go around and FO told atc they gave us a immediate right turn 90 degrees and 4000 feet we did the wind shear escape maneuver and didn't clean up until after 1500 ago and got the plane cleaned up climbing to 4000 and seeing the alert in the top right corner of the guidance panel. Once we hit 4000 I was still hand flying and was inside the plane going in and out of clouds just making sure we were cleaned up and on speed and altitude. FO saw we were getting ready to go into a layer and radiod that we needed an immediate right turn. ATC was very quick and gave it to us I was still handling the plane turning right level at 250 knots and that's when the sever turbulence hit I couldn't control the plane I tried to hold it level but I couldn't t control the pitch or the attitude and I glanced and saw the speed was at 270 knots which we broke 250 below 10 I remember I had the throttles at idle to get it to slow down after about 10 seconds I was able to regain control of the aircraft and continue the turn about a mile later we popped out and it was clear blue skies and smooth. During the turbulence we heard alot of screaming and crying and things floating in the cockpit. I kicked the autopilot on once we out out of it and called in the back to see if there were any injures they said none but the cabin was a mess and the overhead bins opened. FO told ATC that we were just in severe turbulence and we had no injures to report but we couldn't tell if anything happened to the plane is was flying fine at that point. We then climbed to 17000 feet and got vectors to divert to ZZZ2 I made a pa to the passengers and called the flight attendant and told them we're level at 17000 feet about 25 minutes away from  ZZZ2 they asked if they could get out of their seats and close the over head bins real quick I told them they could but use caution and really check and make sure everybody is ok. We  messaged dispatch on our way and they said that ZZZ2 was full and they had no air start cart for us. He told us to slow down as much as we could to buy him some time of finding another ALT (Alternate). ATC was giving us box vectors because we told him that ZZZ2 was no good. I messaged dispatch about 10 minutes later saying we had 5.5 fuel on board and what about ZZZ3 he said just go to ZZZ2 well figure it out on the ground and that he already out ZZZ2 into the system. From the time of the turbulence to getting to the gate in ZZZ2 the cockpit temperature was rising it was about 98 degrees the entire flight before we got to the gate and would not get cold. Landed in ZZZ2 and got to the gate no problem once we shut the engines down the APU and the packs could not keep the plane cool we had passengers still on it but the cockpit rose to 112 degrees and the cabin 92 within 5 minutes of us getting to the gate I deplaned. And was told to call Maintenance Control to make sure I qualify for severe turbulence write up. Called them maintenance came out saw the flap had a bolt broken off. And they canceled the flight 5 hours later.Cause: severe turbulence and windcherSuggestions: don't start the approachTook off from ZZZ1 on our way to ZZZ it was FO's leg as pilot flying he took off and we flew to ZZZ there was a storm approaching the field and act advised that we were gonna be the last plane to make it in they were starting to hold everybody behind us the winds had picked up in ZZZ it was gusting at 30 knots down the pipe pretty much the 6 planes in front of us made it in just fine we were only 4 miles behind the plane in front of us that made it in me and the fo decided that it would be best to swap controls before we started the approach and I would land it we were advised of wind shear on final of plus 20 knots and the advised that the storm had not yet hit the field and was still a couple miles away. Configured just fine I disconnected the auto pilot at 800 feet to hand fly it in was pretty smooth flight till then we got a big gust and were unstable so I called go around atc gave us an immediate right turn and up to 4000 they only turned us at first about 90 degrees we got the plane cleaned up by the time we hit 4000 and we needed another immediate right turn to get in the clear atc at the same time gave us another turn and in the middle of that turn we hit sever turbelance I was still hand flying trying to get us out of the weather and loss complete control of the aircraft for about 10 seconds couldn't maintain altitude or airspeed I did see we were doing 270 below 10 but I couldn't get it to slow down everybody in the back was screaming heard some crying got out of severe turbulence asked fas if anybody was hurt they said no things went flying in the cabin and overhead bins opened climbed to 170000 feet and diverted to ZZZ2 didn't think the plane was damaged it handled fine mx (Maintenance) found a flap bracket broke for right hand sideCause: Hit severe turbulenceSuggestions: Maybe we should have told ZZZ we wanted to hold and not try and land
column123: I was operating Flight ABCD (ZZZ1-ZZZ) as the First Officer and Pilot Flying. The flight was initially delayed due to reported server issues. The Captain contacted Dispatch and I contacted the company for additional information. Dispatch advised that we had approximately 10 minutes to depart before passengers would need to be left in ZZZ1. During pushback; Ground Control advised a normal call for release; however; both the Captain and I questioned this as it did not align with expected flow. While holding short of Runway XYL; we verified on company page that an EDCT (Estimated Departure Clearance Time ) of XA:03 had been issued. The controller responded that he had coordinated with Center and had not received any information indicating a change to our release status.Departure; climb; and cruise were uneventful. As we got on with ZZZ ARTCC; we heard the Center issuing expect holding instructions to aircraft behind us. Based on this; we inferred that we would likely be among the last aircraft to land at ZZZ; and this was later confirmed by ATC.Prior to arrival; we set up and reviewed for the ILS Runway XXC approach; discussing the associated threats and weather conditions. We also reviewed our plan of action in the event of windshear or the need for a missed approach. My captain asked me if I felt comfortable taking the landing; and I said yes. To help mitigate the weather threat; we both had our WX radars up to monitor its movement. ATC informed us that the storm was still a couple of miles from the airport and aircraft were still landing at ZZZ.While being vectored for the ILS Runway XXC approach; we were cleared to intercept the localizer at 4;000 feet MSL. The Captain again asked whether I felt comfortable conducting the approach given the weather conditions and the potential for windshear. After I thought about the conditions; associated risks; and considering my limited experience operating in potential windshear environments; I determined that the most safety-conscious decision was to transfer pilot flying duties to him for the approach and landing. We completed a positive exchange of controls and received our approach clearance after that. The approach controller stated the winds at the field; which at the time no longer had a gust factor like the ATIS. However; we elected the safest course of action was to leave the gust factor in there due to the weather.Upon checking in with Tower; we were advised of a windshear alert in the vicinity of the runway. We elected to continue the approach after considering all the information; including the fact that another  company aircraft was directly 4 miles ahead of us on the same approach; it was still not raining at the airport; and the weather conditions looked safe enough to continue the approach. I observed that company aircraft land and exit the runway without reporting any windshear encounter or other abnormal conditions. Based on the information available at the time; we continued the approach while remaining prepared to execute a go-around if conditions worsened.At approximately 1;000 feet AFE; we began encountering windshear; including rapidly increasing airspeed and updrafts. To my recollection; we gained 100-200 ft and 10-15 kts of airspeed.  We determined the approach could no longer be continued according to our stable approach criteria. Seconds before initiating a go-around; the amber WSHEAR (Wind Shear) annunciation appeared on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). In response; we executed a go-around and followed the Windshear Escape Guidance provided by the aircraft. I remember seeing WSHR (Wind Shear) displayed on the FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator). Around 1500 feet AFE; I told ATC we were going around; and they assigned us a right turn to heading 040 and an altitude of 5;000 feet MSL initially; and shortly after changed it to 4;000 feet MSL. After exiting the windshear conditions; we cleaned up the aircraft and continued to 4;000ft MSL; and got handed off toapproach.As we leveled at 4;000 ft MSL; we were in and out of IMC. Knowing the situation; I told the approach controller we needed a right turn immediately as the IMC cloud layer ended just to the East of our location. The controller said to stand by"; and shortly after that; we encountered severe turbulence for approximately 5-10 seconds before getting a turn to the East. I was glancing inside and outside; but I remember seeing the airspeed increasing. I do not remember the maximum speed of the aircraft. We reported the turbulence encounter to ATC; confirmed with the Flight Attendants that there were no injuries; and coordinated with Dispatch regarding a plan of action. We advised ATC that there were no reported injuries and that we were unable to assess any potential aircraft damage at that time.We elected to divert to ZZZ2; one of our planned alternates; as we believed it would provide the best opportunity for a timely maintenance inspection following the event; and we would not be trying to outfly the weather we just encountered. Once established back in cruise flight; we completed a positive exchange of flight controls.Approximately halfway to ZZZ2; Dispatch advised that an air start cart required for MEL XX-XX was not available at ZZZ2 and asked us to stand by while he looked into other options. To conserve fuel while waiting; we reduced speed and talked about ZZZ3 as another possible alternate due to the services available. After approximately 5-10 minutes; we followed up with our fuel onboard; requested an update on the diversion plan; and asked about ZZZ3.Dispatch advised us to continue to ZZZ2; as the diversion had already been requested and any air start cart issues would be addressed on the ground. The approach and landing at ZZZ2 were uneventful. The only abnormality noted was an unusually warm flight deck during the approach; approximately 80-90° F; with the cabin temperature also beginning to increase after landing.After arriving at the gate; we monitored the cabin temperature and coordinated deplaning once the aft cabin temperature reached 32°C.Cause: The event was caused by convective weather near ZZZ; resulting in windshear during the ILS Runway XXC approach. As conditions deteriorated; our approach became unstable; we executed a go-around following the Windshear Escape Guidance provided by the aircraft. Once in the base turn at 4;000 feet MSL the aircraft encountered severe turbulence associated with the weather. This resulted in a severe turbulence maintenance inspection and damage findings.I believe external pressures may have also been a cause for the event. Safety was always our top priority; however we were already delayed; our dispatcher wanted us to block out; and we were aware that weather conditions were continuing to deteriorate around ZZZ. While these factors in no shape or form compromised safety considerations; they may have contributed to the cause.Suggestions: This event reinforced the importance of erring on the side of caution when convective weather and windshear advisories are present. Although the aircraft ahead of us was continuing to land and conditions initially appeared manageable; a more conservative course of action would have been to avoid attempting the approach.I suggest that crews carefully evaluate not only current conditions; but also trends and the potential for deterioration. In similar situations; choosing not to attempt the approach and instead hold or divert earlier may be the safer course of action. I know I will take a more cautious approach to my weather-making decisions after this; and especially as a Captain."

column121: I arrived at the hangar to perform routine preflight and ground servicing; which included repositioning the aircraft for a planned trip to the fuel farm and performing a ground maintenance run prior to a potential flight later in the day. The aircraft is not equipped with an electrical system or an electric starter; therefore; manual hand-propping is the standard; normal operational method for starting the engine.The aircraft was properly parked on the ramp with wheel chocks securely in place. During the starting sequence from the ground; the engine became flooded and required a clearing procedure. The cockpit throttle control was inadvertently and unintentionally left set open after the clearing procedure was completed.I pulled the propeller through; and the engine fired as expected. However; due to the incorrect throttle setting; the engine immediately produced a sudden; high-power surge of thrust. This surge pulled the aircraft forward tightly against its chocks; causing the tail to lift and the aircraft to nose-over. The propeller struck the ground; causing a prop strike; which immediately terminated engine operation.I was positioned safely on the ground outside the airframe and was never on board or inside the aircraft at any point during the sequence. The aircraft did not move from its parked tie-down location. There were no third-party injuries or third-party property damage. The aircraft sustained localized damage to the propeller; and potentially a wing strut and spar (although the wing itself never touched the ground or any objects). The strut and spar damage likely resulted from the twisting forces and sudden deceleration while the airframe was in a compromised; near-vertical attitude rather than its designed horizontal position. The aircraft was immediately grounded for maintenance inspection; a crankshaft runout check; and repair. The bow in the wing strut was subsequently observed; and the spar inspection initiated; during follow-up visual inspections over the following days.Once the aircraft is repaired; future operations will utilize a secondary tail tie-down restraint system specifically configured to secure the airframe when no auxiliary ground personnel are available to assist with a hand-prop sequence. This mechanical redundancy will back up the wheel chocks and completely eliminate the possibility of a nose-over in the event of an open or malfunctioning throttle. Additionally; a modified ground checklist protocol will be implemented to require a strict physical and audible verification of the throttle; mixture; and ignition controls prior to rotating the propeller. Furthermore; future flooded engine clearing procedures will be performed with the throttle set strictly to the normal 'cracked' starting position; utilizing reverse engine rotations to safely clear excess fuel without exposing the operator to an unexpected high-power surge.

Simultaneously; I assessed available landing options and determined that the most suitable airport was ZZZ Airport.After selecting the airport; I requested priority handling with ZZZ TRACON and advised them of our situation and intended course of action. While maneuvering toward the airport; my student continued working through the engine failure checklist. Initial troubleshooting efforts were unsuccessful; and the engine remained without usable power.As part of continued troubleshooting; I moved the mixture control fully to idle cutoff and then advanced it fully forward. When the mixture control reached the idle cutoff position; the engine began producing partial power. The engine subsequently stabilized at an estimated 40 percent power output. This partial power allowed us to arrest our descent and maintain approximately a 200-foot-per-minute descent rate while continuing toward the airport.We proceeded directly to ZZZ Airport and completed a safe landing under partial engine power. There were no injuries to either occupant; no damage to the aircraft; and no damage to persons or property on the ground.Following the landing; the aircraft was secured and arrangements were made for maintenance inspection to determine the cause of the power loss.

column121: Summary: A near stall/spin accident on the base to final turn that didn't involve poor airspeed or attitude awareness.About the plane: The RV-6A is a side by side experimental airplane. It has a stall speed of about 55 kts; approaches are flown at 70 kts and the maximum flap extension speed is about 85 kts. It has dual controls with the sticks between the legs of the pilot and passenger about 6' behind the front of the knees. There is limited room for the stick and both the pilot and passenger must bow their legs to allow full motion. The flap control can either be electric or a Johnson bar manual control between the pilot and passenger seats. This plane has manual flaps. The pilot and passengers hips are in near contact and it requires reaching between the pilot and passenger legs to pull the flaps. The control is relatively short and the forces make it very difficult to apply full flaps with engine power applied or at any speed above 80 kts.About the flight: The winds were light; sky clear and daytime. I was taking a friend for his first flight in a small airplane as well as his first experience in the cockpit. It was a short flight from my local control towered airport to a nearby uncontrolled field (ZZZ). I did my typical brief as I go with a passenger. I made sure he knew how the seat belts worked as well as how to open the canopy. During the run-up when checking the controls for 'free and correct' I made a point to mention that he should stay clear of the stick between his legs while I was taking off or landing. As I flew to the nearby airport; my friend was enjoying the flight as well as doing some minor maneuvering with his stick.About the incident: I approached ZZZ by entering mid field downwind and started to slow down. I applied the 1st of 2 notches of flaps on downwind. The first notch of flaps doesn't require much effort on my part; but I do have to dig my hand between our legs to get access to the handle. At 1 notch; the end of the flap handle protrudes a little bit above the legs. As I was turning base to final I reached down to apply the 2nd notch of flaps. My friend felt me reaching near his knees decided to helpfully shift his legs away from my hand forcing the stick to the right and locking it in pitch. Note; I'm 5'10' 135#; my friend is 6' and over 200#. I noticed the un-commanded roll to the right. The airspeed was slowing and the AoA alert beeped briefly. I said something to the effect of 'you've got to give me the stick' and he quickly straightened up. I finished the turn and landed safely.How this could have gone bad: If my friend hadn't quickly responded to my request; the intercom wasn't working for some reason or if I had been tongue tied or he hadn't understood the ambiguous request this could have resulted in a stall/spin. Furthermore; to post crash analysis; this would have looked like poor airspeed or attitude awareness even if the logged data was examined.Lessons learned for me: * The terms taking off and landing are ambiguous even to another pilot. I should have announced the phases as I went. Before takeoff; 'stay clear of the stick till I let you know'; start of cruise; 'ok; don't worry about bumping the stick for now'; approach to land 'stay clear of the stick until I let you know'; etc.* I should modify my approach to landing to apply full flaps while still at altitude and in a relatively low workload phase when flying with a non-pilot passenger. * Our passenger stick is locked in with a clevis pin secured with a safety pin. If there is any concern I should always remove the stick for takeoff and landing. Replacing the stick for cruise if I want to let the passenger to try out flying.Suggestions: * During our build; Van's sent a service bulletin to bolt the passenger stick into its socket to prevent it accidentally being pulled out by a pilot flying in the right seat during a critical flight phase. This appears to be trading one risk for another. If used for flight training;the bolt seems entirely appropriate. The stick unsecured may actually be safest if the passenger is only going to do cruise maneuvering.* A statistical analysis of accidents involving between-the-legs sticks as compared to yokes or side sticks would be interesting. An analysis of manual vs. electric flapped equipped RVs may be worthwhile for this particular accident scenario; but there are hopefully not a statistically relevant number.

column121: At the time of the event; the flight crew had been awake for more than 24 hours; having flown over 5 hours; and were completing the final leg of a demanding red-eye trip. Extreme fatigue was a significant compounding factor. Furthermore; as a low-time pilot in type (100 hours); I had not received extensive or standardized training regarding the specific nuances and verification sequence of the Aircraft X parking brake system.Sequence of Events:The aircraft was parked on an inclined ramp with the engines shut down; parking brake disengaged; and chocks in place. The Captain instructed me to set the parking brake. I pulled the parking brake handle; but did not visually verify hydraulic accumulator pressure or the corresponding brake indicator light status. The Captain observed the physical handle position but did not cross-check the system pressure before exiting the aircraft to remove the chocks. No chocks were left behind the wheels to act as a secondary barrier.After re-entering the cabin to secure the cargo door and net; the aircraft began rolling backward due to the incline. Because I was performing pre-flight duties for the next leg and the Captain was focused on the cargo area; the initial movement went unnoticed.Upon realizing the aircraft was moving; I immediately applied the toe brakes; but no braking action was achieved due to a lack of system hydraulic pressure. Ground crew began alerting us to the movement. The Captain hurried to the left seat and also applied the toe brakes with no effect. I attempted to assist by applying passenger-side toe brakes and verbally asked the Captain if I should cycle the parking brake handle forward; I received no response due to the high-stress environment. The Captain subsequently activated the standby hydraulic pump and utilized the steering tiller to steer the aircraft away from immediate hazards; but the aircraft ultimately collided with a parked airframe before coming to a complete stop.Lessons Learned / Safety Recommendations:This incident underscores the critical danger of severe crew fatigue on decision-making and cross-checking procedures. To prevent future occurrences; the exact sequential verification of the parking brake system--including verifying accumulator pressure and indicator lights--must be explicitly taught in training and verified via a mandatory checklist item before chocks are pulled. Reliance on physical handle position alone creates an unsafe latent error.

column121: I was training (CPC getting re-cert time) on SFB and ORL departure satellite with my instructor. Earlier in the session our main transmitter went out on us and we switched to standbys. The standbys are working relatively well and we have no backup frequency. I released Aircraft Y off Runway 7 at ORL who was a WORMS departure (north gate) while also tagging up inbounds for SFB; receiving constant VFR departures off SFB and vectoring other aircraft through the airspace for approaches and over flights. Aircraft Y departs ORL just as I finished talking to a VFR inbound and he checks on and I radar him with a response for the pilot. I go to switch another aircraft to the adjacent sector and they do not respond the first time. This makes me wonder if this frequency is going to go out as well. This frequency we use (125.22) consistently fails and has multiple times over the past months and year. My trainer told the supervisor to tell SFB to put 2 Miles in Trail (MIT) on the SFB departures and less than 30 seconds later I am trying to contact Aircraft Y to climb and turn away from SFB departure corridor but there is no response. I try others and a blind call and nothing. I immediately switch to the orange jack back-up and I get one transmission out to the VFR that answers and then go to climb and turn Aircraft Y and no response. At the same time there is a steady stream of departures already airborne off SFB constantly calling and blocking the frequency so even if I could get out no one would hear me. As I am trying to contact Aircraft Y I also jumped up and tried to get the new URC-300E (replaced the PET-2000) turned on and usable. As all this is going on Aircraft X comes off SFB on his missed approach heading southeast towards Aircraft Y. I am now using the orange jack and the new URC-300E thing alternating transmissions and trying to get Aircraft Y to turn away from Aircraft X because they are wired and then if they miss Aircraft X would be headed into an antenna farm in the southeast. Nothing works; I mean nothing. Mains; standbys; the emergency back-up; the new URC all are dead and all I can do is watch these two aircraft potentially hit each other.Recommendation: The biggest problem we have is the frequencies for this position it fails more often then not and it cannot be trusted. 125.22 is the new frequency we have to replace 119.7 that constantly failed on us but it constantly fails also. This problem has constantly been bandaged and brushed under the rug but it keeps popping up and potentially killing someone. The whole system needs an overhaul now.Another is when we lose either our main or standbys there should be automatic flow in place off the satellite airports. SFB is notorious for launching aircraft really close together and overloading the radar controller and radar screen. You cannot see the targets and the frequency becomes a mess. This needs to stop.After the fact was said technical operations pulled a card. They said they thought Airport Operations Control Center (AOCC) gave them permissions to do so. They should check in the TRACON prior to doing that. But nonetheless it would not have happened if this facility had frequencies that weren't constantly failing they wouldn't have to fix it. This facility is a dump; this isn't the first time this has happened and I am sure it won't be the last. The equipment is not trustworthy and adds extra stress in the operation. Unfortunately nothing will change until two hit.

During this process; I switched the radar to ES (Emergency Service) mode; which began restoring targets. While some scopes started coming back online and others remained dark; all traffic was successfully stopped and contained. The whole event was over in a matter of minutes. Radar and communication failures have happened in Area C multiple times in the last 2 years. The same day earlier in the morning; the area lost multiple frequencies. While we are being continually told the equipment is fixed; issues continue to pop up. We have learned to work out poor frequency coverage areas. We are being a band-aid to a major safety risk in the NAS. If this happened an hour early; the outcome from the level of traffic would have been very different. Im not sure how we find it acceptable to operate with this level of risk of losing radar and communications on a fairly regular basis.

column121: The FO was PF; I was PM. Normal pushback; taxi out. All checklists ran; no abnormal indications. Applied takeoff power. FO rotated (noticed a momentary pause in his positive rate; gear up" call); climbing through roughly 200-300ft; Master Caution for FLT CONT; I looked up and noticed no less than 5 orange lights illuminated. STBY RUDDER; SYS A Low Pressure; 1-2 in that top let panel portion that I can't recall; and bottom right on the Hydraulic panel; both HYD A ENG and ELEC LOW PRESS lights on. I immediately when to the SYS synoptic page to check quantity and pressure. Quantity was full; A was showing 106. B normal. A pressure was rapidly dropping and I saw it bottom at around 400PSI for about 15 seconds. The it slowly came up up. At this point I told the FO to continue flying the airplane; I told ATC; who at this point just handed us off to ZZZ DEP; that we would need to remain at 4000; and stay in the local area. They acknowledged this. At this point I begin to investigate the issue. Quantity was good; pressure on the A side was still low. All lights were extinguished except HYD A ENG. At this point I asked the FO "did you see all the lights"; at which point he said he felt very heavy controls on rotation and "had to pull the airplane off the ground." I went into the FOM non-normals in the iPad and went to Loss of HYD A. The condition is 3 illuminated lights-- all of which were illuminated at one point; and currently just HYD A ENG was still. The FO and I had a quick discussion that this checklist was the safest and most prudent checklist to run. So I began. Completed in it's entirety until it called for the manual gear extension. At this point ATC had cleared us to climb to 6000; and enter a present position hold. The checklist drove us to secure HYD A; and given it's depth; and the condition of the airplane and the FO's input about heavy controls; I both agreed requesting priority handling and returning to ZZZ was the SAFEST path. 175 SOB's and 90 minutes of fuel was relayed to ATC/ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting). Checklist complete; FA's briefed with standard items; PAX's notified of the issue and return to ZZZ; and Dispatch was notified of the priority handling and return. I disconnected wi-fi after the priority handling request and PAX notified. We left the hold and asked for vectors to XXR (longest of the two). The cleared us to join at a 7 mile final. On the dog legged I manually extended the gear and ran the deferred landing checklist. The FO performed the landing; we landed safely and exited the runway and taxied to gate XX under our own power."
column123: I was the PF and everything was normal up to the ROTATE command. The force to rotate the airplane was much heavier than normal. The first pull only lifted the nose of the airplane off of the runway. A second much heavier pull on the control column got the airplane airborne; I felt as though I had to pull the airplane off of the runway. These actions caused a delay in my call for POSITIVE RATE/GEAR UP. Climbing through 200ft agl the captain mentioned the illuminated lights we had in regards to the A hydraulic system. The captain asked ATC for a level off at 4000ft and mentioned the need to possibly return to ZZZ. I was assigned flying and communication while the captain referenced the QRH; contacted dispatch; flight attendants; and spoke to the passengers. A climb to 6000ft and a present position hold was requested by ATC next. In the hold the captain and I discussed what the malfunction was and which checklist would be correct to address the failure and our safest option would be to return to ZZZ. It was also decided that we would request priority handling. The QRH was completed up to point of manual gear extension. After the captain made all the necessary communications with company; flight attendants and passengers; we notified ATC we were ready for an approach to RWY XXR (longest runway available). During the inbound vectors I was rebriefed on the ILS RWY XXR approach and the final checklist items along with the manual gear extension were performed. We were vectored onto a 7 mile final and I configured early to make sure we had no additional problems and made sure we were stabilized early to avoid a go-around after a manual gear extension. Performed a normal landing and taxied off the runway and to the gate. Also want to add fatigue as a threat since we previously flew a red eye with a shorter layover prior to the event.

column121: On takeoff roll; we felt severe vibration that started 120-130kts. We continued our take off with normal procedures. Once established at 10000' per SID; we told ATC about the vibration. ATC confirmed with tower that they saw chunks of tire residues on the runway; and according to their video; we determined that our left main tire blew. Captain transferred aircraft control to the FO and read proper manual. We requested priority; decided to return back to the field; and land on XXL. We contacted dispatch; talked to the FAs and passengers. After setting up for approach and completing appropriate checklists; we got vectored on to final and landed safely. column123: On takeoff on runway XXL from ZZZ at approximately 120-130 knots aircraft started to vibrate significantly with no other indications of a problem. Without a word spoken we continued the takeoff normally and as soon as we lifted off the ground the vibration stopped. We flew the assigned SID and leveled at 10000ft and turned on the autopilot. We told ATC we suspected we had a tire issue and would probably return to ZZZ. We continued climb but stopped at 16000ft with ATC permission. I transferred controls to the first officer and looked up the landing on a flat tire supplementary procedure. After reading it through we decided to return to ZZZ. I sent a message to dispatch; talked to the flight attendants and briefed them on the situation. Informed the PAX (Passengers) of our issue and return to ZZZ. At some point during this time we were informed by ATC that tire rubber was found on the runway and was reported by the previous aircraft. We requested priority with ATC and they gave us a vector to return to ZZZ. We sent a diversion message to dispatch and began to setup the box for the approach back to XXL for ZZZ considering the weather conditions and length of runway. ATC told us it would be a few minutes before the runway was open so that gave time to setup. While in that process ATC told us that they had video of our left rear main gear tire coming apart. So we relooked over the flat tire procedure and decided to land with no auto brakes.We requested landing data but did not receive it so asked dispatch to send us data and confirmed we were good to land and under max weight. We made a normal flaps 30 approach to XXL touched down on the right main gear first. Vibration started again as the left gear touched down but became almost nonexistent at about 50 knots. We exited the runway came to a stop; FO made a remain seated announcement. We were inspected by airport operations and fire crews. They said no smoke; fire or damage and heating of the area was normal. I talked to the flight attendants made sure everyone was seated and made an announcement to the passengers that we would be taxiing back to the gate. We informed ground control and airport ops of our intention to taxi to the gate. Shortly after starting our taxi; maybe 30 seconds; airport ops said company was sending out maintenance and a tow crew. We came to a stop; informed the FAs and PAX and started the APU. After APU start we shut down Engine #1 and looked over the tow in procedure. After inspection maintenance decided; out of caution to tow us into the gate. We were also informed that due to the heavy vibrations on landing that several of the passenger oxygen masks had come down. We were towed into the gate without further incident and wrote up the masks and debriefed. The #2 main gear tire had failed.

column121: On takeoff runway XX winds were 320 at 26 gust 41. The take off below 1000 feet was normal we made a left turn to a heading of 210 climbing to 5000. We brought the flaps up on schedule and level off at 5000. Climbing through 1000 to 5000 we had very strong winds with speed increase to 290 at 5000 with thrust levers at idle. Once the speed came back down to 250 I call autopilot center command. The auto pilot was not able to maintain speed and altitude. I was fighting the autopilot trying to maintain airspeed and altitude we made descent of 300 feet before climbing to 7000 feet. There was a thunderstorm approaching the airport and no windshear warning. Weather change was not reported until after ATC changed airport configuration and we were number one for departure. One corrective action is once the autopilot was not able to maintain airspeed and altitude I should have disconnected the autopilot instead of fighting it.
column123: Upon being cleared for takeoff the tower gave us a left turn heading 210 climb to 5000.  There was a significant change in winds just before departure...winds 210/9...then winds 320/26 gusting to 38...tower reported winds of 320/26 gust 41 (no wind shear warnings) just before taking off.  Climbing out the flaps were retracted on schedule; with a slight delay on the last notch going from flaps 1 to up at about 10 knots above flaps 1 clean maneuvering speed.  Takeoff weight was 356.8 lbs. Climbing through 1000 to 5000 we had very strong winds with speed increase to 290 leveling at 5000; with thrust levers at idle.  Stayed at 5000 for about 2-3 minutes going through some moderate bumps; and strong winds.  Once the speed came back down to 250 autopilot center command was engaged. The auto pilot was not able to maintain speed and altitude. The FO was fighting the autopilot trying to maintain airspeed and altitude...at 290 knots I reported to ATC that we were slowing back & asked for higher; but ATC needed to keep us low....eventually we got a climb to 7000; and direct ZZZZZ. The aircraft descended almost 300 ft before climbing to 7000 with the AP (Autopilot) on.  It seemed like we were kept at 5000 for too long given the turbulence; and weather to the west of the airport; as we were passing to the east of the wx heading southwest.  Later in the flight we were stepped up to FL320; and got a slight course change for some convective activity in the area.  The autopilot was not able to maintain airspeed and altitude due to strong winds & turbulence.  In hindsight I should have taken this leg; but the FO really wanted to fly to ZZZ1 & having flown with this FO before I felt confident in his abilities.  The AP should have been disconnected immediately by the FO & flown manually until safe to re-engage.  I thought I had voiced this as PM; but the FO left the AP on and learned a valuable lesson.  Numerous other aircraft were still taking off & landing at ZZZ.  If needed I would have taken the flight controls; but it never quite got to that point.

column121: Once parked; I am 99% positive I observed the captain pull the parking brake; which is my personal cue to place the transponder in STBY and wait for the shutdown checklist call to begin my shutdown flow. After reading through the shut down checklist; I realized the aircraft had begun rolling backwards and that the parking brake was not on. The aircraft began moving so slowly that I did not notice or feel the movement; as my attention was heads down while completing post flight responsibilities. Thankfully; no one was injured and there was no damage. I'm not positive how far we rolled but my estimate is at least 50 feet. I am 99% confident that I observed the parking brake handle being pulled since it is a flow trigger I have for myself. My best guess is that the brake may not have been in the detent and either slipped out on its own or was accidentally bumped.This event is a stark reminder of how quickly an accident can occur when an action is performed but not positively verified before attention shifts to other tasks. We were not rushing however; it is easy to observe the parking brake handle being pulled and assume it has been properly set before continuing with other duties. All the captains I have flown with have setting the parking brake as pure muscle memory. I do not believe the brake wasn't actually set in the first place. Again; my best guess is it was not fully in the detent. Moving forward I will always verify the brake is properly set before performing other post flight duties. I am extremely grateful that no one was hurt; and this event proves to be reminder of the importance of verification during all phases operation.

If at an airport where there are no people or obstacles prior to the runway; that may be a better place to practice short field landings. In the future I will instruct my students that glide slope is necessary for a safe and stabilized approach to land; even if doing short field landings. Also; having a better briefing of what to do when performing short fields and discussing if we are too low; we should go around; would also be good practice and something to implement.
