column121: I was operating Aircraft X under VFR. Earlier in the flight; I had been receiving VFR flight following from Whidbey Departure before radar services were terminated and I was instructed to squawk VFR. I considered requesting flight following again from Seattle Approach but elected not to because the frequency sounded busy and; during an earlier flight that day; I had not been successful in obtaining the service. As a result; I proceeded without radar traffic advisories while transiting the area.During this phase of the flight; I was descending from 5;500 feet MSL toward a planned altitude of 2;500 feet MSL while simultaneously maneuvering eastbound to remain clear of the 4;000-foot shelf of the Seattle Class B airspace.My planned route took me approximately one nautical mile west of Harvey Airfield (S43). At the time of the encounter; I was level at approximately 3;500 feet MSL. I was not receiving VFR flight following and was monitoring the local practice area frequency rather than the Harvey Airfield CTAF.As I passed west of Harvey Airfield (S43); I observed 2 parachutists descending in close proximity to my aircraft with little advance warning. I immediately maneuvered to avoid a potential collision. Based on my observation from the cockpit; my best estimate is that each parachutist may have come within approximately 100-200 feet of my aircraft; however; I have no objective means to verify the actual separation distance. The encounter was sufficiently close that I believed immediate evasive action was necessary to avoid a collision.I did not hear any 'jumpers away' radio transmissions prior to the encounter. However; because I was monitoring the local practice area frequency; instead of the airport CTAF; it is possible that parachute activity advisories were transmitted on the CTAF and were therefore not received.No collision occurred; and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.Upon reflection; several factors likely contributed to the event. During this portion of the flight; I was managing a descent while navigating to remain clear of the Seattle Class B airspace and elected to monitor an air-to-air frequency rather than the local CTAF while transiting the vicinity of an airport with known parachute operations. Although my route took me approximately one nautical mile west of the Harvey Airfield based on my recollection and review of ForeFlight track log; the encounter demonstrated that active parachutists may be encountered beyond the immediate airport environment. Additionally; although VFR flight following is workload permitting and not guaranteed; requesting it while operating through complex airspace and near known parachute operations may have provided additional situational awareness.This event highlighted for me the importance of proactively reassessing communications priorities when transitioning from en route flight into a congested terminal environment with both complex airspace and known parachute operations. In the future; I will monitor the appropriate CTAF when operating near airports with published parachute operations; will plan my route to provide greater lateral separation from known drop zones whenever practical; and will consider requesting VFR flight following when workload and ATC availability permit to improve overall situational awareness.

column121: During arrival into ZZZ; the flight encountered significant convective weather in the terminal area; resulting in multiple ATC vectors and deviations from the planned arrival route. Following several weather-related reroutes; Approach Control assigned the aircraft 7;000 feet MSL and provided vectors to intercept the final approach course for the ILS Runway XX approach.The assigned vector placed the aircraft on a course that would penetrate a thunderstorm cell. Approach Control subsequently cleared the flight for the ILS Runway XX approach and advised the crew that they were 'cleared for deviations as needed for weather.'While operating in VMC conditions and observing the thunderstorm visually and on airborne weather radar; the pilot maneuvered to avoid the weather. In doing so; the aircraft descended from the assigned altitude of 7;000 feet to approximately 6;000 feet MSL.Approach Control subsequently issued an altitude alert; advised the pilot of the altitude deviation; and reassigned 7;000 feet. The pilot immediately complied and returned the aircraft to the assigned altitude.After reviewing the event; the pilot believes a contributing factor was an incorrect interpretation of the controller's authorization to 'deviate as needed for weather.' The pilot understood the instruction to permit maneuvering as necessary to avoid the convective activity; including vertical maneuvering. In retrospect; the clearance should have been interpreted as authorizing lateral deviations only; with any altitude change requiring a separate ATC clearance.Additional contributing factors included high workload associated with multiple weather deviations; close proximity of convective activity to the final approach course; and the need to make timely weather-avoidance decisions while being vectored for the approach.No loss of aircraft control occurred; weather avoidance was maintained; and the flight immediately complied with the controller's instruction upon notification of the altitude deviation.

column121: We were operating a Part 91 Corporate Business Flight to ZZZ.  This flight segment was operated with two flight crew and no passengers onboard the aircraft.  The flight was operated on a IFR flight plan under Part 91.  The First Officer was the pilot flying for this segment and the Captain was the pilot monitoring.As we began the descent; the current weather information was obtained for the ZZZ area and the visual approach backed up by the GPS XX was loaded into the aircraft GPS / Computers.  The weather conditions at ZZZ were clear below 12;000 feet with winds out of the southwest at 240 - 6 knots.   The GPS XX approach briefing was completed by the First Officer and was to be used as a backup to the visual approach at ZZZ.  The descent checklist was completed as the aircraft descended below 18;000 feet.We were in communication with ZZZ Center as we continued our descent into the ZZZ area.  We requested to proceed direct to the ZZZZZ intersection to set us up for a left base entry onto the final approach for RWY XX at ZZZ.  This was approved by Air Traffic Control and we proceeded direct to ZZZZZ.  Both crew members discussed turning final outside of the ZZZZZ intersection once we had cancelled the IFR flight plan with ZZZ Center.  As the aircraft approached 20 miles southeast of the ZZZ Airport and descended below 10;000 feet we contacted ZZZ Center to cancel the IFR flight plan and proceed VFR.  ZZZ Center advised there one was one piece of traffic possibly converging on the ZZZ area and that we would arrive prior to them based on aircraft speed.  ZZZ Center approved the frequency change and advised squawk VFR.  We scanned the traffic on our Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) and observed one aircraft northeast of the ZZZ area that did not appear to be a factor for our approach.  A check of the map utilizing ADS B data on the foreflight map did not reveal any traffic in the area.  The final portion of the descent checklist was completed as the aircraft passed through 10;000 feet and the sterile cockpit announcement was made.  All external lights were illuminated at this time as part of the normal flow when operating below 10;000 feet.The frequency change was approved and we began to transmit our position and intentions on the ZZZ CTAF.  Numerous radio calls and announcements were made of our intentions to enter a left base for Runway XX at ZZZ.  The First Officer selected Heading Mode and began to maneuver the aircraft for an extended left base for a final approach to Runway XX.  I continued to make radio calls announcing our position; altitude and intentions.  Upon nearing and making a radio call of the extended left base entry for Runway XX; we heard a radio call by a vehicle on the ground crossing the runway at ZZZ.  I made additional radio calls announcing our position and intentions upon entering the left base entry for Runway XX.  We heard another radio call from the vehicle announcing they were clear of the runway at ZZZ.  I completed another radio call stating we were turning a 7 mile final approach for Runway XX.  There had been a couple of very weak and nearly unreadable radio transmissions from an aircraft stating ZZZ1 which is to the southwest of the ZZZ airport.  No other radio transmissions were heard by me or the First Officer.  We obtained one final wind check from the ZZZ weather system indicating the winds were now 210 at 5 knots.  I informed the First Officer of the updated winds and we began to configure the aircraft for the final approach and landing at ZZZ.  The First Officer stated that he had observed a target momentarily pop up on the MFD northwest of the airport but then disappeared.  I scanned the center MFD along with the First Officers MFD and no traffic was present.  This is commonly observed in that area as there are numerous helicopter operations occurring around this airspace.  The aircraft was fully configured and the landing checklist was completed prior to reaching 1;000 feet.  I made several more radio transmissions as we continued the final approach segment to Runway XX.  The 1;000 foot callout was made and the aircraft stable response was given as the aircraft was on speed and the proper glidepath for landing utilizing the GPS approach as a backup.  I began to scan the runway environment and the MFD to ensure the area was clear.  I announced a reflection from what appeared to be a vehicle near the far end of the runway holding short on the taxiway.  I informed the First Officer this was likely the vehicle that had previously crossed the runway and I would continue to ensure they did not enter the runway environment.  Upon scanning the MFD there were no targets or aircraft on the screen anywhere in the area.  The 500 foot callout was made notating aircraft speed; sink rate and stable criteria.  A continuous scan outside of the aircraft revealed the area was clear as we neared the runway.  Touchdown occurred around the 1;000 foot markers and the aircraft began to decelerate normally.  I began to make normal landing callouts indicating that the ground spoilers were deployed and the aircraft was continuing to decelerate.  As the aircraft was continuing to slow on the back half of the runway; the First Officer stated ' Oh ---- there is an aircraft on the runway '.  As I looked up; I observed an experimental type aircraft on Runway XY proceeding the opposite direction.  The First Officer steered the aircraft to the right side of the runway and the opposing aircraft had also steered to the right side of the runway.  Our aircraft speed was estimated between 40 and 60 knots as the other aircraft passed us.  We continued down to the next taxiway and exited the runway.I made a radio call to inquire if the aircraft on the ground at ZZZ was on frequency.  A male subject stated yes; he was on the frequency.  I asked the subject if he had made any radio calls at ZZZ and he indicated he had.  I informed him we had made numerous radio calls and had not heard one call from him and that he needed to have his radio checked.  Upon exiting the runway someone asked if the runway had been cleared.  I made a radio call announcing we were clear of Runway XX per normal procedure.  Just as we exited the runway; we observed the same experimental aircraft taking off the opposite direction on Runway XX and no radio calls were made regarding the departure or any other intentions in the area.  We continued our taxi to the ramp at ZZZ and completed our shutdown procedures and checklist.  The vehicle which was stationary short of the runway on the taxiway proceeded to the ramp and we began to speak with them about the occurrence.  Both individuals in the vehicle are certificated pilots and both stated that neither one of them had heard any radio transmissions from the experimental aircraft.  I inquired if they heard our radio transmissions and both individuals stated they heard our radio transmissions inbound to the runway.  The individuals indicated that the experimental aircraft proceeded to hurry down the runway and made a quick 180 degree turn and immediately started to take off.  They did not hear any radio transmissions from the aircraft either as it rapidly departed.  Neither individual was able to obtain a registration number on the experimental aircraft and no further radio transmissions were heard after the aircraft departed.The First Officer spoke with the Airport Line Technician regarding the occurrence. This appeared to be the only aircraft operating in the area near the time of our arrival.  Upon searching the website it appeared the aircraft proceeded to the ZZZ1 Airport and landed. It is unknown if the faint and weak radio transmissions we heard was from the experimental aircraft and they were incorrectly stating ZZZ1 or if the aircraft landed at the wrong airport.No traffic alert or notifications were transmitted by our aircraft avionics; nor did we ever observe any aircraft on our MFD.  No traffic alerts were received with the ADS B information via Foreflight which was active on both iPad's at the time of the occurrence.

column121: After our runup; we began to taxi to RWY XX.  We realized that we were converging on  a tail wheel RV who was taxiing towards us.  We slowed down and the RV pulled over by the hangars just north of the ramp.  After passing him; we both believed that he was going to the southern runup area for some kind of testing.  Now holding short of XX; we waited for the aircraft that had just departed XX to get far enough before taking the runway ourselves.  2 airplanes holding short behind us; 2 made radio calls maneuvering for the 45; and 2 in the pattern all for XX.  Clearing the downwind; base; final; and runway we lined up and began our takeoff.  I heard a non airport specific radio call that said 'RV you have another airplane taking off opposite runway'; however we did not hear a radio call for the RV departing XY.  At this time I could not see the far end of XY due to the middle of the runway elevation being higher than either threshold.  Seconds later I saw the same RV on the end of RWY XY.  My brain reacted faster than my mouth possibly could.  I yanked the throttle to idle; applied hard braking; and then my mouth caught up to yell ABORT 3x.  We came to a stop on the thousand footers for the end of RWY XX.  I took a few moments to seek suitable options to get us to safety.  Taxiing to the next taxiway; roughly 600 feet closer to the aircraft coming towards did not seem like the safest option.  Turning around and getting off the first taxiway didn't seem like the best option either as we would have to turn our back to them and would lose visual on them.  The airplane rotated well before us; and somewhat side stepped to the east of the runway.  We waited until they were well clear of us and initiated another takeoff.  We then departed the area to the south.  Upon returning the RV was leaving the ZZZ ramp again and momentarily started taxiing to XY again.  We had just cleared the runway as they made a partial radio call 'Aircraft Y is taxiing to RWY uhhhhhhh....'.  They stopped at the south exit of the ramp.  RWY XX was still in use.  We slowed down more south of their location; having just passed the south ramp entrance.  They corrected and turned for XX.  I believe that a contributing factor to the RV's confusion could have been the aircraft that took off RWY XY approximately 10 minutes prior led them to believe incorrectly.  The departing aircraft made a radio call confirming RWY XX should be used and everybody scattered to switch to RWY XX. Several aircraft had made calls and even a few had landed/taken off RWY XX from that time to time of event.

column121: On Day 6; I conducted a Part 107 photography mission at Location X.I had originally checked the airspace for this location on Day 0; when I was first notified of the assignment and observed no permanent airspace restrictions affecting the operation. I did not recheck airspace status immediately prior to launch on Day 6.I launched my DJI aircraft and conducted approximately 15 minutes of photography and videography around the property and adjacent area. No geofencing or authorization warning was presented at initial startup or takeoff.After landing; I initiated a second flight to capture additional footage. During this process; a geofencing warning appeared on the controller. After takeoff; I reviewed the warning more closely and realized it referenced a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR). While hovering; I checked my airspace application and confirmed that my operating location was within the affected area of the TFR. Upon recognizing the conflict; I immediately terminated the operation and landed the aircraft. No further flights were conducted at the location.This was my first encounter with a stadium-related TFR. My previous experience obtaining authorization for controlled airspace operations had primarily involved LAANC authorizations associated with airport airspace. As a result of this event; I will incorporate a final airspace and NOTAM/TFR review immediately before every flight; regardless of whether the location was previously checked during mission planning.

column121: I submitted a Part 107 LAANC flight authorization earlier in the day to capture aerial imagery at Location X (controlled airspace). After preparing the aircraft; a coworker expressed interest in flying; and I agreed to let him manipulate the controls while acting as Pilot in Command (PIC).I requested takeoff clearance via a LAANC provider but inadvertently accepted the application's default next-5-minute increment (XA:35) instead of the immediate window (XA:30). My attention shifted heavily to preflight duties; supervising an inexperienced person; and visually scanning the local area to maintain safe separation from non-participating crowds and obstacles within a tight 30-foot operational bubble.The drone was launched at XA:33; two minutes prior to the active authorization window. The discrepancy was caught upon post-flight log review. No manned traffic was in the area; and visual line of sight was maintained at all times. During the low-altitude (12-30 ft) flight; non-participating children began chasing the aircraft. I initially maintained safe lateral separation; but immediately terminated the flight and landed when they began running and standing directly underneath the aircraft; sometimes actively reaching for it.Contributing Factors: High cognitive workload introduced by supervising an unrated person while establishing a safe flight perimeter. Additionally; my background in manned aviation accustomed me to flight plans being opened dynamically via two-way radio upon request; rather than strictly adhering to automated; fixed-time blocks used for LAANC approval. I was aware that LAANC worked in time authorization blocks; but I erroneously believed I was approved for the current time block. I am also accustomed to pre-flighting well in advance of the takeoff window for manned aircraft; a habit that translated poorly to a rigid digital block system.Hardware design and human habits also contributed: I was utilizing a phone-display controller that lacks a native timekeeping element on its Head-up Display (HUD). Because my smartwatch was malfunctioning; I was effectively locked out of verifying the current time once the controller connected to the sUAS. Finally; I relied on a memory-based preflight inspection rather than a structured; written checklist; which allowed the LAANC time-verification step to be missed during a high-workload scenario.Future Corrective/Mitigation Actions:Defer connecting the drone to the controller until the approved LAANC window is actively confirmed as current; unless a reliable; independent timekeeping device is available at the control station.Transition from a memory-based preflight inspection to a formalized; written checklist. This new checklist will be explicitly updated to include hard steps for checking active LAANC authorization windows; ensuring adequate timekeeping equipment is available; and assessing localized environmental safety issues; specifically accounting for dynamic pedestrian traffic--such as children--who may actively seek to place themselves directly under the drone's flight path.

column123: Coming in on the ZZZZZ arrival at 6000ft on the down wind. ATC told us to slow to 190kt and to descend and maintain 4000 feet. I started a descent. During the descent at around 5000ft; ATC instructed us to turn right to heading of 100° and maintain 2000ft. I increase the rate of descent and deploy flight spoilers to help. ATC then cleared us for the visual approach and instructs us to turn to a 170 heading to intercept the course. On the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) it looks as if we would intercept right around the FAF fix. We were still flying at 190kt maintaining the airspeed to keep a good descent rate. Captain requested a 120 heading to give us a little more time. We turned back left slightly and continued the descent. ATC then advised us; that due to the new turn that we are now below the Glideslope and that the next fix on the approach is 3000ft. I selected V/S and reduced the vertical speed to -200 ft./min. Captain selected 3000ft in the Mode Control Panel (MCP); but also selected ALT HOLD to try to assist in a very busy period. I saw the 3000ft in the MCP; but did not recognize the ALT HOLD selection. At which point I looked at the MFD to gain situation awareness of the approach; and the Aircraft began to pitch up to return to the altitude that was captured for ALT HOLD. The Speed Brakes were still out and the thrust was at a lower setting; and so airspeed bled off quickly. Once I recognized what had happened; I immediately grabbed the controls to push the nose forward and increase the thrust. Due to the surprise of the sequence of events; I only managed to select the Autopilot disconnect once. After a few moments though; I got the auto pilot horn off; and I stowed the speed brakes. The aircraft sped up; and after a some adjustments; stabilized to a normal attitude and airspeed. We brought the gear down; and set final approach speed. The speed continued to decrease towards target; and we were stable by 1000ft and 500ft. The landing; touchdown and rollout were uneventful.

At this point; the Gear lowered normally; all 3 Gear Extension Lights illuminated; and I terminated the checklist. Since corrective action had already been initiated; I continued the climb; ensured positive terrain separation; and repositioned the aircraft back onto a safe and stabilized flight path for the visual approach. The landing was completed without further incident.At no time during the event did ATC provide a warning regarding proximity to terrain or obstacles; nor was any pilot deviation issued or communication received advising unsafe separation. No damage or injuries occurred.Contributing factors included ATC vectoring for a visual approach; interpretation of a 5-mile base instruction; compressed maneuvering space; and increased workload during descent and configuration. column121: FAA Part 107 Certificated Pilot since 2017. We have worked in every class of US FAA airspace across 28 states. We operate and adhere to strict safety cases and internal policies with our authorizations. On this day detailed below; we observed what we believe to be several UAS violations; unsafe operations and both UAS and crewed aircraft in close proximity to Location X as well as UAS nearby not yielding to crewed craft. We are certain we saw UAS flying over 400'+ AGL; BVLOS and failure to yield to approaching crewed aircraft. Despite the presence of large crowds; we witnessed one personal aircraft; flying very low at Location X; which we estimated to be 50-75' above structure at one point in question and climbing and diving over large crowds to more closely view the event described below.On the morning in question: I traveled from our corporate offices to Location X in order to attend; photograph and video the event. We never expected the crowds that rapidly gathered. There were probably over 2500-3500 people; primarily confined in two large locations.The planning for this trip began as a personal / company photography mission but after speaking with our company contacts; we were contacted by a past client; who mentioned that companies would be interested in seeing and possibly purchasing a copy of any footage obtained. We took several drones to photograph with and we were going to decide upon arrival which to use given the observed factors on-site but we decided on the DJI Mavic 2 Pro utilizing the DJI Smart Controller RM500. The drone is FAA registered and Remote ID (RID) compliant. This decision was made for a couple specific reasons; the most prominent being that the airspace was becoming notably congested with aircraft and drones approximately 15 minutes before the event start. In the pre-planning for our flights; we witnessed two aircraft that would arrive; circle and depart; estimated to be well over 1500-2500 feet AGL (may have been higher) and two drones scouting the location as we did within an hour prior to the event. We began launching from East of Location X due to better light but with other drones present; we decided we were too far from Location X (noting some UAS must likely be flying BVLOS). We relocated to the west of Location X where we would be within 100-200 feet of our drone and looking up at blue-sky at all times. At that time; we did seek out and met two other UAS pilots before the event and discussed VLOS and avoidance coordination. Unfortunately; despite our coordination efforts with others; in the 30 minutes prior to the event; with our one (1) and three (3) other nearby drones up; we noted that two aircraft in particular were circling (on about each occasional third or fourth pass) too low for us to even risk to continue flying UAS at this location. Despite the large amount of people still arriving and large crowds; planes were flying very low (which we videoed as it seemed to be at times just 100-200 feet above the structure at Location X) at one point a private aircraft seemed to be about 50' above the structure. We decided at that time not to fly. Soon; the two low flying aircraft began to fly much higher and well above the structure (it seemed to us that they likely spotted the drones hovering near the top of and well-over (probably 75-125' over the surface) so the low-flying; circling manned aircraft began to climb. We also noted that drones that were launching both from the East side and west of the structure and were flying over it. This was notable to us immediately because we have noted it elsewhere as inexperience - while they were likely within 400' of their takeoff point (controller reading) they were well above the structure; which would mathematically put them well over 400' or even 500' AGL despite the readings they would have had observed within 400' vertical of controller altitude. (I've always felt this is something the FAA needs to teach better as many rely on the 400' alt. controller reading). With the planes now flying much higher; knowing we would be well within giving-way to them; and would stay below structure height; we took flight after discussion of our plans with two other UAS pilots nearby. I had one individual helping me to maintain safe takeoff and visualize safe launch as there were people nearby including children (highly curious); which we wanted to be sure did not approach upon launch and I had a nearby visual observer as there was sun glare upon moving to the structure's westerly location. In anticipation of the event start; at approximately XA:57; I launched with a new battery (95%) and positioned to begin capturing photos and video of the event start. As I hovered in position around XB:03 the event started and we began recording and photography. Immediately upon event start; I noticed not the original 2-3 aircraft but now as many as two additional (4-5 total) private aircraft suddenly circling with one flying exceedingly low again and so I called out my altitude to my VO (about 25-45 feet the structure) and immediately said I would descend to structure level or below top of the structure to give-way. I also noted not two other UAS (we coordinated with) but now (at times) as many as 8-10 (estimated) drones. One zipped past traveling at a high rate from West to East. I estimate this was 15-20 feet horizontally from me and within 5-10 feet vertically; flying approximately 40 MPH (possibly closer as we observed on my video afterwards). We began to discuss landing and scrapping our plans as several drones were flying sporadically; circling and changing altitude abruptly. My VO noted that several of us were in coordination but a few of these MUST be flying strictly through their controller screens from afar; out of VLOS because they were very close to us vs. our visual (blue-sky) VO / VLOS practice / technique; looking up. 13 min. 41 sec. into my flight we became more concerned. At event start; UAS (Data: 181' above launch; approx. 225' AGL; approx. 200' from controller; est 150' horiz feet from the structure) with 35% battery remaining; two (2) drones approached us and came within several feet to my hover (unacceptable and unsafe proximity in my judgement of their speed and proximity) given the way they approached. One was behind and moving left to be between my drone and I; one near and about 50' above with another approaching. With trees below; I was worried that I had no route to home point remaining with a drone between me and mine; and I typically land with 20% battery remaining to be safe. At that time; I pushed in towards the structure; thinking if I got trapped with low battery; I could land safely on the unoccupied structure and retrieve the drone after it was clear OR drop below the drones; to above tree level and turn for home point. However; knowing there were crewed aircraft potentially above (albeit well clear) other UAS hovering behind; UAS left and one above; I pushed in towards the structure (Data: 186' above launch; approx. 230' AGL; at 300' from controller; approx. 50' distance from the structure) with 30% battery remaining; I stopped to hover to assess the RTH path I could take (or land). At that time; with no stick input (and confirmed none made in subsequent review of data and control inputs) I looked at my screen to confirm location and I was level with the top of the structure (or slightly above). I said to my VO; 'we have to land up there or am I clear of the others to return?' and he said I don't see you. I looked up and couldn't ascertain my drone from several others that had moved in around mine; when I looked down at the screen to regain orientation; the drone was still moving towards the structure despite no stick inputs. At this time; the screen froze. In that moment; the interpretation by myself and my VO of the situation was that despite stopping to hover at about 50-70' from the structure; I had either been struck by one of the other dronesand dropped to trees below; or without my input; the drone had continued forward and was on the structure; and/or had collided with the structure; or more unfortunately; people. I was concerned for their safety and had a concern for battery fire (having worked on wildfire drone teams; this is trained to be a primary concern upon crash) so I initiated our procedural lost-link / disconnection procedure (screen grab photo; note direction of travel; check controller link; look for possible ground fire etc) but could not retrieve UAS contact or location. The last location was ON the structure surface; which made me think a drone had collided with us; the drone had continued forward and collided OR lost link and initiated Emergency Landing. It was set for RTH but it never came back; which reinforced our fear of a crash. I immediately took phone photos of surroundings and the structure. I reached out first to nearby pilots (2); all of which still had full control and VLOS with their UAS. There was no way to contact other drones because they were flying in from afar; pilots unknown. I reached out over the next 10 minutes to law enforcement. Each thanked me and confirmed they had no calls from workers or persons on-site. Law enforcement then gave me permission to access the structure but only after traffic from the access road; and hundreds of cars and thousands of people cleared. They said I could be trespassing or stopped by officials but if called they noted to their agencies that I was going up on a nearby road to walk the structure and if called; they would know it was me. Approximately an hour later; I found the drone on the structure. It had most likely collided with the concrete wall of the structure and was damaged. Someone; I'm assuming the workers; had picked the damaged drone up and placed it upright atop one of the concrete walls (clearly positioned so that anyone coming up to search could see and find it) and it was not at a place where it could have landed given the damage encountered. The drone had no oil; paint; fabric or blood on it; so I don't believe there were injuries. The props did receive spinning damage; so I believe it went in under power; with forward flight damage (front). It did have concrete fragments and concrete dust on it; so I believe it contacted the structure. I tried to contact the company to be sure nobody was contacted; struck or injured but at this time; my calls have not been returned. I did report back to law enforcement to thank everyone for their help and support and let them know I confirmed no battery fire; retrieved the UAS and they noted my calls. I have not been able to confirm that there were or were not any personal injuries.We did retrieve the drone fairly intact but damaged; with all video; photos and flight data onboard and retrieved. The drone was not recording at the time of contact. The last photo was taken at the point where I paused (released sticks to neutral / last stick inputs at approximately 50-70' off structure). There were no other stick inputs after that but we estimate over the next several seconds that based upon trajectories; GPS data and onboard telemetry that the UAS flew on for 0'+/- vertical and 50-60' horizontal before contact / collision and loss of data and radio contact. The last speed reading was at 15.8 MPH horizontal forward with no stick manipulation. Proximity and anti-collision avoidance sensors were not turned on during flight. We can't ascertain if there was any contact to or from other UAS prior to contact with the structure; but all sensors were nominal with exception of the movement / forward acceleration w/o command; which is likely the cause of contact. We are not sure if the radio signal (forward motion) could have been interfered with or overridden by one of the other nearby UAS controllers. That is obtainable by reading the manufacturer's .DAT file which we do not have the software to extract or read.  We fully debriefed and analyzed a

column121: I was the remote pilot in command of a 14 CFR Part 107 small UAS operation conducted under a LAANC authorization with a maximum altitude of 100 feet AGL.  The operation was located approximately 3 miles Northeast of ZZZ at approximately XA:00 on Day 0.  The purpose of the flight was to capture video of a private construction project nearing completion.My prior Part 107 experience in controlled airspace has primarily involved DJI Phantom and Mavic aircraft used for construction mapping and site progress photography; often on automated missions. This operation used a homebuilt first-person-view (FPV) small UAS. I was operating with a visual observer who is also an experienced FAA Part 107 remote pilot.Before the first event; my visual observer reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity of the operation. I initiated a high-rate climb. Shortly after the climb began; the GPS-derived altitude displayed in my FPV goggles indicated approximately 172 feet AGL; or approximately 72 feet above the 100-foot LAANC authorization. I immediately initiated recovery by reducing throttle; rolling the aircraft inverted; and commanding a descent back toward the operating area.During the recovery descent; the aircraft's FPV perspective indicated that it was descending; but the displayed GPS altitude continued to increase and briefly indicated approximately 272 feet AGL before becoming inconsistent and then decreasing. Because the altitude indication was GPS-derived and appeared to lag or behave unreliably during the high-rate climb and recovery; I cannot determine the aircraft's actual maximum altitude with certainty. However; I believe the aircraft exceeded the 100-foot LAANC authorization; and I immediately continued the descent and landed. The altitude exceedance appeared to last approximately five seconds. After the aircraft returned to low altitude; my visual observer again reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity.I did not intend to deviate from the LAANC authorization; and I took immediate corrective action as soon as I recognized the altitude exceedance. Contributing factors included unreliable or delayed GPS altitude indication during a high-rate climb; limited visual altitude references in the open area; and my underestimation of the climb performance of the FPV aircraft relative to the 100-foot authorized ceiling.Corrective actions have already been taken. I configured audible altitude warnings and altitude callouts on my radio transmitter. Before future operations I will review and set those warnings with a significant buffer below the authorized ceiling. For 100-foot LAANC authorizations; I will use a substantially reduced personal maximum altitude rather than operating up to the LAANC ceiling. I will also avoid high-rate vertical climbs in low-ceiling LAANC airspace.A second altitude exceedance occurred later in the same operation; several battery packs later. I activated the GPS Return to Home / GPS Rescue function in the same open operating area to observe its routing behavior. During the automated return; I realized the aircraft was climbing toward and then above the 100-foot LAANC ceiling. I attempted to override the automation with stick inputs; which changed the aircraft attitude but did not stop the climb. I then deactivated the return function by switching back to full manual control. I observed a maximum displayed GPS altitude of approximately 128 feet AGL; or approximately 28 feet above the authorized altitude. I immediately descended and landed. This altitude exceedance also appeared to last approximately five seconds. My visual observer reported that he did not observe any aircraft in the vicinity.During debrief; I realized this second event likely occurred because my GPS Return to Home / GPS Rescue function was configured to return at the maximum altitude recorded during the flight session. I had configured it this way to avoid an incorrectly preset return altitude. However; I misunderstood how the Betaflight flight controller defined a flight session. I had kept the flight controller and GPS powered during main battery changes using a USB battery pack so that GPS lock would be retained. I now believe the flight controller treated the later battery pack as part of the same flight session; meaning the return altitude was based on the maximum altitude recorded earlier in the operation rather than only the current battery pack or arming cycle.Although I chose the open field because it reduced collision risk with ground obstacles; I did not adequately account for the risk of testing an automated flight aid under a low LAANC ceiling in controlled airspace. I will not test GPS Rescue; Return to Home; failsafe behavior; or other autonomous flight functions within LAANC-controlled airspace or other altitude-sensitive airspace unless the full test profile remains safely below all applicable altitude limits. Future testing of these functions will be conducted in suitable airspace with a larger altitude margin.These events highlighted gaps in my understanding of my aircraft's altitude indication; climb performance; flight controller session behavior; and automated rescue configuration. The most important lesson for me is that open terrain on the ground does not mean the airspace risk is low. I will use these lessons to improve my preflight planning; altitude margins; automation testing procedures; and overall aeronautical decision-making to better protect the airspace and the people living and working beneath it.

column121: We operated Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ2 on Day 0. We departed late due to the weather in ZZZ and a minor maintenance issue on the ground. Upon reaching our cruising altitude of 17;000 ft both the CA and I simultaneously smelled a strong odor of something electrical that was burning (noxious and acrid). It was only a second or two before it became very strong and we immediately donned our oxygen masks; established crew communications; and followed the instructions in the QRC. We re-established that I would remain the PF and the CA would handle the radios; QRH; etc. The CA then advised ATC and reported a burning odor in the flight deck and requested a diversion to ZZZ1. I agreed with that decision given the weather we had just left in ZZZ and the weather we were dealing with at the time; and I remembered that during our pre-departure briefing we had both pointed out that the weather near ZZZ1acuse (to the east) was better than in ZZZ or to the south.The CA worked on communicating to ATC and Dispatch (via ATC); as well as to the FA and the passengers while I continued flying the aircraft. ATC began giving us descents and headings to bring us onto the approach to runway XX. It was difficult to establish meaningful communication with the FA because the oxygen masks are so loud; as well as the fact that the noise from heavy rain on the windshield was quite loud as well. We had trouble hearing him and he had trouble hearing us; but we were able to at least communicate that we were diverting to ZZZ1 and that there was no smoke in the passenger cabin.The CA continued working through the QRH during the descent toward the airport in heavy rain; IMC; and moderate turbulence. We jointly decided not to depressurize the cabin given the fact that there was no reported smoke or fumes there.We accomplished our remaining checklists and were eventually vectored onto the approach for runway XX; whereupon we broke out of the weather; picked up the runway lights; and landed in heavy rain without incident. Emergency vehicles met us on the taxiway and followed us to the gate; where firefighters entered the aircraft to inspect for smoke and we were able to deplane. EMS wanted the CA and I to deplane first for treatment; but both the CA and I were uncomfortable with leaving the aircraft before the passengers so we waited until the plane was empty to leave the flight deck. EMS then treated me and the CA and said we both had high blood pressure and heart rates; which is to be expected after a stressful event like this. We were both nauseated and somewhat light-headed as well; but again that was to be expected given the odor and the stress of the situation. Several passengers were seen by EMS as well for anxiety.In the end; I believe the CA and I handled the situation correctly and professionally; that we followed our training; and I am thankful for the safe outcome for everyone involved.Root cause narrative: Acrid; burning odor which smelled like something electrical was burning.
column123: A few mins after reaching our cruise altitude of 17;000 Feet; the FO and I smelled an acrid electrical odor on the flight deck that quickly became stronger and overpowering. The FO continued flying the aircraft and I followed the QRC steps to don our oxygen masks and establish communication over the speakers. Once communication was established between us; I advised ZZZ Center. We had 51 souls and 5500 lbs of fuel on board the aircraft. I looked at divert options. The ZZZ airport was about 60 behind us with marginal weather and heavy rain showers. ZZZ1 was slightly closer and had better weather and a longer runway; so I informed ZZZ Center to give us direct to the ZZZ1 airport; which they did. I also asked them to contact our dispatcher/operations and let them know of the divert. I contacted the FA through the cabin emergency mode of the intercom; but because the oxygen masks were so loud; we were having trouble hearing him. I asked several times if the FA had any smoke or odor in the cabin. Finally; the FO heard the FA say no smoke or odor. We were initially cleared down to 11;000 feet. The FO continued flying and I gave him the radios while I ran the QRH. I accomplished the initial steps on the QRH but stopped short of depressurization because I didn't feel it was warranted; with no odor in the cabin and no visible smoke of any kind. I also decided not to isolate the electrical system or turn off any generators as we were in heavy rain showers and IMC and I did not want to compound the issues; given it was an odor and we were not dealing with smoke or fire.At this point we were given 4;000 feet and handed to ZZZ approach. We descended below the weather shortly after this and took the ILS into RXX. Emergency vehicles met us on the taxiway and followed us to the gate where we met firefighters. They tested the air quality on the flight deck and we deplaned using the main cabin door. The FO and I felt nauseous and were checked by EMS and released with no further symptoms other than elevated blood pressure. Several passengers were quite anxious and also evaluated and released.

column121: During preflight prep; ATIS was advertising noise abatement procedures for departures.  Both the FO and I checked the Jepps 10-9; as well as the airport company pages departures notes for noise abatement procedures and found none.  We both failed to reference the Jepps 10-4 page.Our ATC clearance was Make a left turn to join Aircraft Y; climb to Level 300; and Squawk XXXX".When we were cleared for takeoff; there was no mention of the noise abatement procedure.  In hindsight; I feel like previous departures the controller has issued the clearance of "Fly runway heading until 2;500 ft and then left turn on course; you are cleared for Takeoff".  This tower controller simply gave us "Cleared for Takeoff" with no further instructions.We began our left turn on course after passing 400' AGL.  During the turn; the tower controller reminded us in the future to fly the published noise abatement procedure.  This was ultimately our mistake; but I feel misled by the way the airport company pages and the Jepps are constructed for BGI (TBPB).  At other airports with noise abatement procedures; (Aruba for example) the Jepps 10-9 or 10-9a has the noise abatement procedure published on the airport diagram.  It is absent from the BGI 10-9.  In the airport company pages; every other airport I can find has a bold NOISE ABATEMENT section if procedures apply.  In the BGI airport company pages there is no such designation.  There is a line in red that reminds pilots to comply with departure restrictions; however there is nothing indicative of a Noise Abatement procedure."

column121: Hot Summer day leaving ZZZ on Aircraft X. We were heavy with fuel because of needing a precautionary alternate. There were long lines of thunderstorms through the northeast en route and at the destination. We had to run numbers for passengers and bags due to weight restrictions. In order to takeoff  we needed to burn fuel off to make takeoff weight restrictions. We were also calculating out through landing weight restrictions. For the first leg I was pilot monitoring and the captain was pilot flying. During the takeoff roll at approximately 80 knots the engine indicating system for Interstage Turbine Temperature (ITT) engine one went red. I let about 3 seconds pass debating on calling for the reject before V1. I observed the ITT go back to normal temperatures and decided not to call reject before reaching V1. On climb out after the takeoff checklist and getting the auto pilot on I informed the captain of what I had observed. On review of SOPs I realize I should have verbalized the indication immediately but hesitated due to there being no annunciation. Throughout the flight we continued to monitor the ITT temperature gauges. We noticed engine 1 ITT consistently 40 degrees higher than engine 2. When the pilot selected climb one we observed ITT 1 nearing overheat so we backed off the throttle to climb 2. Nearing the top of climb we similarly observed ITT 1 nearing limitations reaching FL280. Similarly after leveling off and beginning to accelerate to 290 temperatures began spiking and nearing limitations. We slowed to cruising at 270 to avoid an exceedance. After landing in ZZZ1 the landing exceedance warning pops up and we ran the QRH. After getting to the gate in ZZZ1 we write up the excedence and maintenance (MX) come out to perform an inspection. After the inspection maintenance said the operations check was good. Leaving ZZZ1 the captain and I discussed threats leaving and the plan with another potential ITT 1 excedence. We speculated hot temperatures in ZZZ and near max weight as being causes and since we were lighter and If temperatures were lower it would be less likely. We tried to coordinate for a takeoff on XX for runway length in case of a rejected takeoff but ATC had difficulties coordinating it with staffing. We accepted XYL for takeoff. We also decided to do the TO with no flex to increase runway remaining if needed. I was pilot flying from ZZZ1 on this flight. During the takeoff roll we observed ITT 1 turn red exceeding temperature limits again at around 80 knots.  The Captain called the reject and took controls. We notified ATC and returned to the gate. Maintenance came out to the aircraft and perform and another inspection. Stated the exceedence were within limits and ops checked it clearing it for flight. We refused the flight since no other mx was done and they would not perform a run up of the engine.

column121: I was the Pilot Flying (PF); and Pilot in Command; and Person A was the Pilot Monitoring (PM).  We departed for ZZZ.While being vectored for the RNAV approach into ZZZ; I called for the landing gear to be extended. Person A selected the landing gear handle down and observed a green indication for the left main landing gear only. The nose gear and right main landing gear did not show green indications. The landing gear handle light was not illuminated red. Person A made the callout that only the left main landing gear appeared to be down and locked.I initiated the missed approach and Person A advised ZZZ Approach of the landing gear indication issue and requested vectors to allow time for troubleshooting. Person A retrieved the abnormal landing gear checklist and began working through the procedure.The checklist directed us to complete the emergency landing gear extension procedure. The crew discussed the available options and elected to divert to ZZZ1 due to maintenance availability at that location and better weather. We decided to leave the landing gear configuration unchanged because we could not confirm the position of the nose gear and right main gear; and we did not want to further change the aircraft configuration prior to completing the emergency gear extension procedure.During the descent into ZZZ1; Person A advised ZZZ Approach that we would be completing the emergency gear extension checklist and requested a level-off and airspeed reduction to approximately 150 knots. ATC confirmed we were experiencing a landing gear issue and asked if we wanted to request priority handling. The crew agreed that priority handling was appropriate.The emergency landing gear extension checklist was completed; however; the nose gear and right main gear still did not provide green cockpit indications. We coordinated with ZZZ Approach and ZZZ1 Tower for a low approach so the tower could visually verify the landing gear position. The tower reported that the landing gear appeared to be down.Person A pressed on the landing gear indication button multiple times and he was finally able to get a green light for the Nose gear.  This led me to believe it was more of just a light indication issue rather than an actual gear issue.    After completing a circuit in the pattern; we elected to land. The landing was completed without issue. We exited the runway and were escorted back to parking by Airport Fire Rescue.Cause:  Landing Gear Indication for Nose gear and Right Main were not indicating down.Suggestions:  Have a way to swap or replace landing gear indicator lights in flight on the BeechJet.

column121: Skies clear; 10 statute miles of visibility. Visual Approach at ZZZ with another pilot in the right seat. I was flying the C-172 in the left downwind when ATC requests I make a short approach for runway XX. I accepted and landed the plane prior to the thousand foot markers. To make taxiway 1; I had to use the brakes to slow down. Upon initiating the turn onto the taxiway; both main tires went flat. After both tires went flat; the aircraft became unmovable and stuck on runway XX. I immediately told ZZZ Tower that I was unable to exit the runway and airport operations closed for approximately 30 minutes from a period of about XA:10-XA:40pm. The aircraft was moved onto the ramp and airport operations resumed at approximately XA:40. In hindsight; I believe that I made the mistake of initiating the turn onto taxiway 1 too soon. The aircraft was likely moving too fast and my judgement to utilize the breaks instead of rolling past the taxiway contributed to the event. I should have kept rolling and gotten off at the end of the runway on taxiway 2. Ultimately; the aircraft never left the paved surface of the runway and taxiways. The only damage was to the tires and tubes of both main wheels; which were replaced approximately 2 hours later. There were no injuries.

LNAV is already engaged; but I failed to select VNAV on the MCP.  Crossing DARIC I direct the PM to set touchdown zone.  I configure aircraft with the 4 and 2 mile rings around SUNEY to be fully configured.  Between GREYZ and FONZI I can see the PAPIs for RWY 15 indicating  2 red and 2 white.  I've used those to monitor and cross check my path on the River Visual.  It isn't until approaching JUBOL do I realize we're low.  I try to take a peak at legs page to see what altitude we should be at; but unable to see that information.  I get a GPWS aural OBSTACLE".  I disconnect the autopilot and pitch the nose up and add power.  PM calls out to watch my airspeed.  I add more power and we climb higher and accelerate.  I didn't hear the radio call from tower stating "altitude alert" because I channelized getting back on airspeed and path.  When I began picking up the PAPI for Rwy 19 I could see 3 red 1 white.  I corrected to 2 red 1 white."

column121: Operating flight #ABCD ZZZ-ZZZZ1; everything was good on preflight and blocked out on time. Taxied to runway XXL and without much delay took the runway for takeoff clearance around XA:30PM. Normal takeoff and on positive rate called for gear up. EICAS caution C HYD Demand Pump came up along with PRESS light on overhead panel. A few seconds later Gear Disagree EICAS came on momentarily but cleared as we continued the climb. ATC gave us a few turn instructions for traffic conflict and then cleared up to 10;000 and to switch to ZZZ Departure. Once with Departure control; priority was requested and a level off at 10;000ft with radar vectors was requested. Flight control was transferred to the FO while I ran the QRH along with the Relief Pilot. Once the QRH was done; we contacted dispatch and Maintenance Control to confirm correct QRH was referenced. The decision was made to return to ZZZ. ATC was advised that we would dump fuel to get down below overweight landing weight and better performance for stopping on runway. Dumping started at XA:52 and ended at XA:57 at 10;0000ft. Dispatch was notified of location. Flight attendants were briefed and the passengers were notified of our planned return to ZZZ. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) was requested on arrival and notified of possible hot brakes. Normal ILS approach and landing on XXR with a rollout at the end. Cleared the runway and stopped for Hot Brakes on the right gear showing 5 in the caution range and waited for the 15 minutes to see if they would continue rising. Temperature decrease was noted and a taxi to the gate was commenced. Upon arrival at the gate; Maintenance was briefed. We then went to the Chief Pilot for a debriefing with the Crew.

column121: Engine failure at cruiseWhile cruising at FL300 there was a sudden bang and the number two engine began to spool down. There were no warnings indication prior to this. I initially began to run the memory items for Engine Fire Severe Damage checklist but soon realized that the engine had basically shut down. There were no fire or Eng (Engine) vibration after the engine shut down. I moved over to the Engine Failure Shutdown checklist and started running that after advising ATC and requesting lower from ATC. The engine out altitude was 24;000 feet but we were given clearance to 14;000 feet. The FO was flying while I ran the checklist. ZZZ airport was approximately 40 miles due East of us while ZZZ1 was about 240 miles in front of us. I decided to proceed to ZZZ. I briefed the flight attendants and spoke to the passengers. While completing the checklist It was extremely busy while we were setting up for the approach but manageable. Weather was clear and calm and the plane flew fine on one engine. We landed normally but with flaps 15. I calculated we were about 3100 pounds over Max gross landing weight. The touchdown and rollout were all normal. We came to a gradual stop on the runway and waited for the fire trucks. The fire trucks came onto the runway and did an inspection. They told us they could see the number two engine was not running and that there was no sign of fire and all was clear. We then continued to the gate single engine without incident. ATC and ZZZ Airport were all very supportive and helpful throughout the whole incident.
column123: We were cruising along at FL300; about an hour and a half into the flight to ZZZ1. I was the PF; the captain was PM. There was a sudden loud pop sound accompanied by a slight yawing motion of the aircraft as the #2 engine started rolling back. There was a startle factor for a few seconds while we both scanned the engine stack to assess the situation. The captain beat me to the throttle controls and pulled the #2 throttle back to idle. By the time he had done that; the ENG FAIL amber annunciator was displayed on the engine display. Knowing we had just experienced an engine loss; the captain advised ATC and coordinated an immediate descent. I clicked off the autopilot and began handflying the descent. I noticed on my display that ZZZ was almost right underneath us; and before I could recommend that I believe ATC offered it as a landing site. Captain agreed and we started planning. I put the #1 engine at max continuous thrust to slow the descent. I did this because we got a vector away from the airport and I didn't want to dive aggressively losing altitude while moving away from our landing field; and to buy us time to run checklists and coordinate with everyone. Everything felt controlled and smooth; granted there was a sense of urgency given the situation and we had no idea what had caused the engine to fail randomly. There were no previous indications that a failure was imminent. I kept flying and took over the radios so the captain could coordinate with the FA's; notify the passengers of the situation; and started running QRC and emergency checklists. They were using XXR at ZZZ so the captain set me up quickly for that runway in the FMS and the radios. Later ATC told us to plan for XXL; so we set up for that runway instead. He ran the applicable engine failure checklists; referenced and briefed me on the Flaps 15 approach; speeds; distances; go-around; etc. I had to accomplish a 360 degree turn in the descent as we approached the airport environment as we were still too high even after I'd pulled #1 back and started descending faster. ATC had cleared the area out for us so we had clearance to maneuver however we needed. Captain had finished the checklists right about the time I had the aircraft stabilizing on the centertline and glidepath for XXL; roughly around 3000 ft if I recall correctly. I configured the aircraft earlier than I usually would so I could make sure it was trimmed and stable well before we got too close to landing. The landing was uneventful; in the touchdown zone; deployed the one running engine reverser; and the captain took the aircraft as we rolled to a stop. He set the parking brake and had CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) look our right engine over and make sure there was nothing going on with it before taxiing. We'd had no high temperature abnormalities or fire indications in the air so we were fairly confident it was fine; but in the interest of safety we wanted verification before clearing the runway and taxiing to the gate.

column121: I was serving as the Remote Pilot in Command (RPIC) for a Part 107 security-related UAS operation conducted on Day 0; at Location X. Prior to the operation; I obtained a LAANC authorization for the operating area. The operation was conducted approximately XA:50-XE:01 at altitudes not exceeding 300 feet AGL. After the flight was completed; I reviewed the authorization details and discovered that the LAANC authorization had been approved for XM:15-XQ:15 rather than the morning operating period. The incorrect time period resulted from an error during the authorization request process and was not identified during the preflight review. During the operation; the flight remained within the authorized geographic area and below the approved altitude. Weather and visibility conditions were suitable for flight. No conflicts with manned aircraft; ATC communications; injuries; property damage; equipment malfunctions; or other safety events occurred. column121: At around XA:30; we had a full T1 communications outage while Aircraft X was enroute transitioning over our airspace. We noticed our long range radars went into the red in our radar Status Information Area (SIA). We immediately tried our external shout lines; which we found to be unresponsive. The radar controller then noticed that we lost radar contract with our other enroute transitioning aircraft; because they were too far from our local radar to pick up without fusion. The controller correctly said radar contact lost. We might have lost radar on Aircraft X as well; post-situation we aren't positive. I attempted to landline call upstairs to the tower where our supervisor was; but the phone line was dead. I physically sprinted to inform them. During this moment both I and the radar controller failed to see that Aircraft X was extremely near the boundary with ZID. We attempted the Interim Voice Switch Replacement (IVSR) dial line with ZID but it wasn't working. Finally the T1 communications seemed to come back; as I pick up the landline phone and I immediately called ZID supervisor who got the ZID controller to take the handoff. The handoff likely occurred with less than appropriate separation from the boundary. There would be another T1 communications outage less than an hour later which caused another unsafe event to occur which will be in a different report.Our equipment is NOT consistently reliable for the safe transition of aircraft in our airspace. We have outages constantly including these major T1 communications outages; and we seem to allow it simply because we often have low traffic; such as this instance with only two aircraft. But it only takes an unfortunate circumstance to realize that keeping our bar for safety so low is an extreme negligence to our flying public.At around XB:10 we had a full T1 radar and communication outage. We lost: our external dial lines and shout lines; Flight Data Input/Output (FDIO) uplink; we lost our fusion long range radars; our landline phone line was dead (eventually we could landline dial intrafacility). At the time thankfully we had no aircraft. Due to the communication outage I had to physically tell the supervisor.Eventually our intrafacility landline phone worked; so I communicated with our now two supervisors in the tower; who told me we were likely going ATC limited or zero. Due to weather we had no aircraft in our airspace; much of the airspace was IFR. At XB:20 called the supervisors again because we had two satellite IFR departure proposals both of which would immediately be entering ZID airspace and thus would require coordination which we could not do; AND these satellite airports were at the edges of our northern airspace where we likely couldn't provide radar service since we were on primary radar only. At XB:29 Aircraft Y called requesting to pick up his IFR off PMH. The FDIO was down; so we had no flight plan; and we had no external communication capability to get it even though we still had the airspace. I called to the tower; a supervisor told me to just send him to ZID. We switched Aircraft Y to ZID even though he had to climb 10k feet through the heart of our airspace which we technically still controlled even without operating equipment for the last twenty minutes. It's possible that Aircraft Y was attempting to call us on the ground for his IFR via the landline; which was interfacility out of service; and no pilot could know that our TRACON inoperative.One hour prior to this event we had an additional T1 full communication and radar outage which eventually returned but the outage caused an unsafe situation to occur.We should have a procedure to make a decision faster to close the TRACON. Waiting on the district and Air Traffic Manager (ATM) to tell us what to do is slow and unsafe.Our equipment is NOT consistently reliable for the safe transition of aircraft in our airspace. We have outages constantly including these major T1 communications outages; and we seem to allow it simply because we often have low traffic; such as this instance with only one aircraft. But it only takes an unfortunate circumstance to realize that keeping our bar for safety so low is an extreme negligence to our flying public.

column121: On my recent ZZZ ZZZZ ZZZ paring; SATCOM datalink was lost as soon as we lost VHF radio coverage on both legs. These two legs fly in Datalink Mandated (DLM) airspace. On the ZZZ ZZZZ leg; after losing SATCOM datalink; we contacted Maintenance Control via SATCOM as the phone feature still worked. They were unable to provide any guidance on how to remedy the situation. The person we spoke with also stated that he wasn't very familiar with the system. ZZZZ control was adamant that we relog in" to CPDLC which we couldn't without the datalink. They reluctantly accepted us into the airspace via voice operations and we were able to relog into CPDLC once we were in VHF coverage. After landing in ZZZZ. The maintenance technician reported this was a "common issue" with the B737 and reset the system for the outbound flight.On our return flight; on a different tail number; the same thing happened. I again was able to contact dispatch using the SATCOM as that feature still worked. I again was concerned with operating in the DLM airspace without datalink. Dispatch stated we would have to exit RVSM airspace; descend to FL280; and divert to ZZZ1 only to land with very little fuel (5;300 lb.). I then asked him to contact ZZZZ1 and ZZZZ control centers and ask if we could operate on our current route and at our current altitude without datalink. The dispatcher did so and replied that the control centers approved the request "since we lost the datalink airborne;" ultimately saving the flight from a costly divert. We also contacted Maintenance Control again and they said there was no way of resetting the system airborne. During the preflight; we referenced the 737 operations guide that provides a photo of the SATCOM page that should be checked (this information should be put in the Flight Manual (FM)). Our page matched the picture; but once airborne; PS VOICE stated "unavailable." This is how I knew we would lose the datalink once out of VHF coverage. The FM provides no reference to what these prompts on the Swift Broadband (SBB) page of the SATCOM feature in the Control Display Unit (CDU) indicate or any troubleshooting guidance. This situation created quite a distraction for the flight crew when operating in the region for both legs and is a safety concern."

column121: Aircraft X operated from CLT to ZZZ without any operational irregularities other than two encounters with light wake turbulence shortly after departure.Following departure from Runway 36R at CLT; we departed behind a B737. During the initial climb;while established on the SID and flying approximately heading 025; the aircraft encountered light wake turbulence consistent with the preceding traffic. The disturbance was minor and did not result in any significant deviation from assigned altitude or heading. Aircraft control was maintained at all times. Shortly thereafter; ATC assigned a heading of 310 degrees and instructed us to contact Departure. During the turn to the assigned heading; we encountered a second brief episode of light wake turbulence; again believed to be associated with the preceding B737. This encounter was also minor in nature. The aircraft remained fully controllable; and there were no abrupt aircraft movements; exceedances; or operational concerns. No injuries were reported; and the remainder of the flight proceeded normally without incident.Upon arrival at ZZZ; after the passengers had deplaned; the Flight Attendant advised me that a Captain [from another airline] seated in 1A had requested to speak with the flight crew. The passenger identified himself.While still in the flight deck completing post-flight checklist items; I heard the Captain attempt to return up the mobile stair ramp toward the aircraft door while the First Officer was retrieving items at the door. I heard the First Officer advise him that he was required to remain on the tarmac and could not come back up the ramp.I met with the Captain after deplaning. He asked questions regarding the flight and inquired who had been flying the aircraft. I explained that I had been serving as Pilot Monitoring and that the First Officer had been the Pilot Flying.The [other airline] Captain then attempted to speak with the First Officer while he was conducting the post-flight exterior inspection. The First Officer advised that he would complete his assigned duties and return afterward. The Captain appeared displeased with that response. During our discussion; Captain stated that he had never experienced such an abrupt turn" and expressed that he was interested in seeing what the FOQA data would show regarding the event; including how many Gs the aircraft had experienced. I advised him that; from the flight deck's perspective; the aircraft had encountered only light wake turbulence and that the resulting movement was minimal. At no point did the wake turbulence result in a loss of control; significant deviation from assigned altitude or heading; or any indication that aircraft limitations had been approached.I was surprised by the level of concern expressed given the relatively minor nature of the wake turbulence encounter. I was further concerned when a Flight Attendant informed me of comments allegedly made by Captain during cruise while in the presence of passengers. According to the Flight Attendant; the Captain expressed his concerns openly and in an unprofessional manner while she was walking through the cabin. From the flight crew's perspective; the aircraft encountered two brief episodes of light wake turbulence during the departure phase. Both events were managed appropriately; aircraft control was maintained at all times; and the remainder of the flight was uneventful."
column123: Route Charlotte Douglas (CLT) - ZZZThis report documents unprofessional conduct by [another airline] Captain who was traveling asa non-revenue ('nonrev') passenger on Aircraft X. This configuration meant non-crew personnel had no legitimate reason toreturn to the aircraft door area once on the ground.Sequence of Events1. The First Officer instructed him that hewas required to remain on the tarmac and was not permitted back up the ramp to the aircraft perpolicy.3. Confrontation with Aircraft X Captain: Aircraft X Captain went down to the tarmac to address theindividual directly.4. Attempted approach to First Officer during post-flight walk-around: When the First Officercame down the ramp to begin the post-flight exterior inspection; the Captain called out that theFirst Officer needed to come speak with him about the takeoff. The First Officer advised that heneeded to complete his duties; and continued the inspection; noting that the Aircraft X Captain was alreadypresent to address the matter.Departure was from Runway 36R. Per the SID; the aircraft turned right to a heading of 025. Shortlyafter; the flight encountered slight wake turbulence from a 737 departing ahead. ATC then instructed aleft turn to heading 320; during this turn; the flight again encountered mild wake turbulence.The combination of the SID-mandated right turn; the subsequent ATC-directed left turn; and briefmild wake turbulence produced some perceptible turning and minor wobble. This was a normal;mild encounter consistent with published SID procedures and ATC vectoring around precedingtraffic. There were no abnormal indications; no exceedances; and nothing rising to the level of anoperational concern. No safety event occurred and no report to ATC; dispatch; or maintenancewas warranted based on the turbulence itself.As a non-revenue passenger; the Captain was traveling as a guest of the airline and had nooperational role or authority on the flight.Airing complaints to other passengers and the flight attendant during theflight was unprofessional and had the potential to needlessly alarm fellow passengers about a non-event.Returning to the secured ramp/door area after deplaning; when passengers are required to remainon the tarmac pending transport; was a deviation from ramp safety procedure.Attempting to summon the First Officer away from required post-flight duties (walk-aroundinspection) to litigate a non-issue was inappropriate; particularly after being told the Captain wasavailable and present to discuss the matter.Wearing a uniform while nonrevving does not confer any authority over crew;operations; or another carrier's aircraft; and the individual's manner suggested an assumption ofauthority he did not have.No safety issue resulted from the takeoff itself. Aircraft X Captain addressed the individual directly on thetarmac. The First Officer declined to engage further and completed required post-flight duties. I determined which taxiway was Q by elimination; not runway 12/30 and not P by their differential lighting; white runway and red closure. column121: WHO/WHAT/WHERE/WHEN/WHY: I am a Part 107 certified remote pilot. On Day 0; I conducted a brief commercial UAS flight using a DJI Air 3 to capture roof photographs for a solar installation. The operation took place at Location X; which is located in Class B airspace approximately 6.5 NM from ZZZ airport. The flight path also briefly and inadvertently clipped the extreme outer lateral edge of an active TFR.CHAIN OF EVENTS & CAUSE: On the day of the occurrence; I had a demanding schedule with multiple marketing shoots across different locations. I diligently performed pre-flight airspace checks for every other site throughout the day. However; due to task saturation and a momentary lapse in situational awareness at this specific location; I mistakenly assumed the airspace was clear and inadvertently omitted both the LAANC authorization and the local active TFR NOTAM checks prior to launching. I launched the drone manually; climbed to approximately 38 feet AGL directly over the private property; captured the required photographs; and landed safely within 13 minutes. No manned aircraft or other hazards were present; and there was no conflict. The oversight regarding both the Class B airspace and the outer edge of the TFR boundary was discovered post-flight when reviewing my flight logs and airspace charts.HUMAN FACTORS & CORRECTIVE ACTIONS: The primary root cause was human error stemming from complacency and fatigue due to a high volume of consecutive shoots on site. To prevent any future recurrence; I have updated my standard operating procedures to shift all airspace and NOTAM/TFR analysis to the pre-trip planning phase. Moving forward; I am mandating a proactive desktop airspace assessment and securing advanced LAANC scheduling up to 48 hours prior to leaving for any field site. This ensures all flight boundaries and authorizations are locked into my calendar beforehand; removing the pressure of performing critical safety checks during the rush of on-site setup.
