column121: Due to low staffing numbers AVP; radar positions have been combined to the tower cab outside of mid-shift hours. This has been expected of us by upper management to facilitate operating the facility with 50% staffing. During the winter months when traffic volume is low is quite a different situation than now in the summertime when traffic volume is high. We've done this for years; as it was common practice when I arrived to the facility. The current SOP allows the practice but has requirements for notifications to management outside of the building if it is done outside of mid-shift hours. District management was advised this would have to become standard practice until staffing numbers increase and has elected to forego the phone call and consider a daily log entry as sufficient.On the date and time above; I was instructed to work a session on North in the tower cab. It was early afternoon and a typical busy time. Traffic was moderate and complex with sequencing to the primary airport; a mix of IFR and VFR overflights; plus Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z flying around the airspace sightseeing. I also had multiple flight school airplanes in the practice areas. I don't recall if I had any practice instrument approaches at that time. At least SERMNs (SWAP (Severe Weather Avoidance Plan) Escape Routes - Metro New York Area) or PHLYRs (Philadelphia area weather avoidance routes) weren't active. I don't think I stopped talking for the 90 minutes I was on.I was busy enough and uncomfortable enough that at one point I grabbed another CPC who was not on position at the moment and just told him to keep an eye over my shoulder. He assisted with landline coordination and making amendments for me as Ground Control (GC) was defaulted to covering Arrival Data (AD) functions; something that isn't covered by SOP. The trainee in question is certified on both GC and AD but is otherwise not a CPC. I was forced to manually coordinate routing for one or two aircraft because the trainee wasn't able to complete amendments I needed correctly and in a timely manner. It took him close to 10 minutes to amend a VFR's altitude so that I could hand off to the correct sector. I have no clue what the exact issue was with that; or what other traffic he had on Ground at that exact time. AVP was busy as a whole so there were definitely airplanes that required attention outside of the window. Working arrival data is a heads-down position and completely contrary to what a ground controller should be doing. This particular day was unique in that AVP was using both of our intersecting runways due to winds and traffic.To further complicate the session; while I was working with frequencies directly in my ear; many times I had trouble hearing pilots talking to me because of other speakers in the cab. There were low clouds moving in from the west forcing most of my VFR traffic that was flying westbound to continue to descend lower and lower to maintain VFR; which only put them in the middle of our arrival and departure corridors.Upper level management almost expects us to combine to the tower in order to operate the facility and accomplish training. I understand that realistically the ONLY way to get out of the staffing crisis is to train and certify controllers. I feel we've reached the point where doing this is inherently unsafe. The safety of day to day operations rest solely on the shoulders of the small handful of FPLs (Full Performance Level) on the shift. We're outnumbered daily by partially qualified and newly position-certified trainees. There are often times where an FPL on radar has had to correct a situation on local; or the Controller in Charge (CIC) has had to step in; or even an FPL who is on technically on break has to step in.When combined to the tower cab; we are forced to sacrifice a lot in terms of redundancy and basic safety. There is no voice switch bypass for radar frequencies in the tower cab. This has been brought up to tech operations foryears already. There is only one Interim Voice Switch Replacement (IVSR) that radar controller can use and no spare that someone can plug in and help coordinate in a pinch. GC is defaulted to work AD functions and when training is underway on a new trainee that adds undue burden on both the trainee and the trainer as they don't even have a concept of what is happening in the airspace. The Tower Display Workstation (TDW) is 1/3(?) of the size of a Terminal Controller Workstation (TCW); is washed out as soon as someone bumps a window shade open.In the moments we're told to train then it feels like the trainee and I could share a chair. The small scope means I need to stand nearly in their lap to be able to even see the scope. Meanwhile; the doubling of people required to train crowds the room quickly. There have been many instances where we're training on all 3 positions at the same time. Sure it looks great on the Cru-ART (shift log); but at what cost. What is the benefit of teaching new people bad practices from the start? What is the benefit of working without a basic backup to our radios? What is the benefit of doubling the heads-down workload of a trainee who should be looking out the window? What is the benefit of forcing a trainee to complete AD functions when they haven't even received classroom training on it? What is the benefit of putting all the above-mentioned responsibility on the shoulder of the few FPLs on the shift?Recommendation: At this point I don't know what would be the most effective change to implement. We need more than 50% staffing. We can't continue to be pushed to exhaustion by 60-hour workweeks just to have basic staffing in the building. We can't be expected to work radar combined to the tower until further notice. We should not be forcing trainees to endure decades of bad decisions while they struggle to learn to separate airplanes.Adding a full TCW has been brought up in the past but adding just installing a new screen without an addition IVSR or even so much as a bypass for the voice switch is a waste [of] time and money. Splitting off AD from GC won't work because we don't have enough IVSRs or so much as enough counter space.Forcing trainees to sit on position even if there's no traffic but also rushing them to check out sooner continues to rob them of the quality training.

column121: After a moderate to heavy volume of arrivals; Aircraft X was one of the last in the sequence. They were coming from the south-southwest; and had the field in sight about 18 miles out for AVL. I cleared them for a visual approach to Runway 35. A moment later; Aircraft Y; who never called Approach for services (we looked up the callsign that was tied to the ADS-B to find out the information on the aircraft) departed 0A7 northwest bound and then turned to the left and was climbing at a good rate. Thankfully for everyone involved; I had not shipped Aircraft X to the tower yet as they were descending in for the visual approach. Since I've seen this exact scenario play out numerous times; I cancelled the Aircraft X's visual approach clearance and had them continue on present heading followed by a right turn; and right when they crossed the 051 MVA boundary; I had them maintain 050 because I had another aircraft in the right downwind for Runway 35 at 060. Aircraft Y continued to climb; oblivious to the fact that they were flying right through our final for AVL at a dangerous altitude. Aircraft X was cleared for the visual approach 35 after passing behind the VFR aircraft.Plenty of luck was involved here that avoided any major deals or potential midairs. If I had simply shipped the Aircraft X to the tower when they were 13 miles out; which is not unreasonable; the potential for a midair collision would have been significant because Aircraft X would have been in frequency transition during the critical moment; and Aircraft Y had no need to or desire to call Asheville Approach for services because they were legally outside of Class C airspace still. Luck was involved with me not descending the aircraft on the right downwind to 051; which would have been a standard thing to do. If Aircraft Y had decided to depart a few minutes earlier; when my traffic volume was much greater; including many VFR aircraft flying around in and around downwinds that I had to maneuver all of my arrivals around; I may not have noticed their departure as quickly as I did now.Recommendation: Similar reports to this have been filed multiple times over the many years that I've worked here by many different controllers. The AVL Class C needs to be changed to not allow 0A7 departures to fly under the Runway 35 final approach course at dangerous altitudes. As it stands; it is LEGAL for VFR aircraft to cross UMUXE at 040 and not violate the Class Charlie; which is EXACTLY the published altitude for crossing that fix on the RNAV 35 and the ILS 35. The FAA has been made aware that this is a HIGHLY DANGEROUS situation on numerous occasions and the only feedback the FAA has ever given the controllers at AVL is that changing the Class Charlie would require an act of Congress" AKA it is too hard/too much effort for management to do. The FAA spends plenty of time monitoring and figuring out how to reduce CPC breaks and other useless behaviors; there is plenty of time for them to do ACTUAL WORK and fix the AVL Class C airspace. One day; if nothing changes; all of the wrong luck will happen in this KNOWN AND WELL REPORTED ON UNSAFE AIRSPACE/PROCEDURE that will cost people their lives. If that ever happens; let it be known that this safety issue was reported on numerous times and something could have been done about it."

column121: On Day 1; I was exposed to a disturbing circumstance that I feel should be corrected for the benefit of pilots and safety. My cross-country journey began at ZZZ in the morning of Day 0. I had a passenger; an experienced cross-country land and sea pilot as well as a photographer. We were loaded with gear for our journey to ZZZ1. To stay within weight requirements; we were limited on fuel capacity which required us to make several short flights from airport to airport for fuel stops.We stayed overnight at ZZZ2 that night after taking a tour of the lake for photos. The next morning; we toured another lake for more photos. As we continued our journey to ZZZ1; we took the opportunity for more photos of rivers and lakes on the way. More fuel stops were made along the path.Arriving at Coeur d'Alene Lake; we toured for more photos and noticed the Sea Plane Base (S76) had two planes and a ferry boat docked and there was no room for another plane. We decided it would be best to fuel at COE; a non-towered airport shown on the current Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) sectional chart.After checking the AWOS at COE channel 135.075 for wind and other information; it favored Runway 20 for landing. With no additional comments; I switched to the UNICOM channel 122.8 as indicated on the sectional chart and announced my intentions five to six miles out that I was approaching and planned to overfly the airport 500 feet above the pattern altitude to verify the wind to Runway 20.During my approach; five miles out to the space COE; I did notice one aircraft departing to the west. Otherwise; there was no other traffic in the area after checking the windsock and verifying that Runway 20 was best wind for land. Also noticed there was no traffic in the air or on the ground. I announced that I was maneuvering for a mid-field crossing to enter left downwind; for Runway 20. After turning downwind; I made another radio call stating I was on an extended downwind for Runway 20. I lowered my landing gear and flaps; then announced I left base for Runway 20. I established a stabilized approach and announced final for Runway 20.Immediately after touching down; I heard a radio call about switching to 120 something? I exited the runway at the first taxi exit and headed for what I thought was the fuel area as there were Phillips 66 signs. Then I got a radio call asking my intentions. I responded that I needed some fuel. The controller told me that it was a towered airport now and I needed to switch to 120.125 frequency. I told him I had no idea as the current FAA chart indicates a non-towered airport with fuel. He said it was on the NOTAM and I made a mistake. He instructed me to taxi down to the run-up area of Runway 02 for further instructions. He told me that this has been a common miscommunication with pilots for a while.After fueling up for our last leg to ZZZ1; I called ATC for progressive taxi instructions to the tower for better explanation. The tower was a bit difficult to see or find as it was a makeshift setup of container boxes stacked up. After climbing to the top of containers where the controllers were; we had a nice cordial discussion regarding the lack of information available to incoming pilots. Not only is it not on the currently published sectional FAA charts; but it's also not on the NOTAM. The simple solution is to have it announced in the AWOS recording until the charts are updated. Additionally; the UNICOM channel should be monitored by ATC to give pilots the correct frequency as they enter the COE airspace and do not wait until after they have landed.Furthermore; I hope that your organization can be of some help to me in this particular case. As I take aviation responsibilities very seriously and don't want this to be a blemish on my record. I am not sure what I could have done differently except going to a different airport.In conclusion; I hope for the safety of all and the fairness of other pilots; the continuation ofthis problem at COE must be corrected; regardless of their growing pains.

column121: On Day 3 I performed a drone flight to capture photography as part of my professional duties at the request of my employer. The organization I work for includes over a mile of outdoor space accessible by the general public; therefore internal drone flights and protocols are managed by the organization's robust safety and security team. The flight area included Class G air space I'm familiar with and know the flight rules for. A flight plan was submitted and approved more than 3 days prior to the flight; as is our organization's protocol; and our safety and security office was again notified of the flight via phone just before launch. Flight time and area were picked for a non-populated time to ensure all safety protocols were in place regarding any bystanders. The drone was launched at roughly XA:00 and in flight for roughly 8 minutes when I was approached by law enforcement officers who asked me to land the drone and informed me of a TFR in the area. I immediately cooperated and landed the drone and spoke with the officers; answering all questions. They informed me I was on the edge of and just entering a temporary flight restricted area that had earlier been established -- I had no prior knowledge of this TFR and informed them as such. Furthermore; neither DJI's 'Before You Fly' map nor the drone's geofencing advisory warning system alerted me to the TFR area. I informed the officers that I was flying as documentation for my employer and neither I nor my organization were aware of the established TFR for that date; and have been granted an FAA Waiver 14 CFR § 107.39 for flights over human beings (though the flight did not occur over any people) and our safety and security team has submitted information to authorities for waiver/approval to fly in the same area in which the organization is restricting external drone access for a large event occurring the next week. It is unclear whether this waiver has anything to do with not receiving a notice via DJI of a restricted area; or just the apparent unreliability of the geofencing and advisory system of the application - as it was explained to me that the remote ID information provided for the waiver would prevent such messages from occurring on the day of the scheduled event. The officers were understanding and took my information and proceeded on; informing me not to fly the drone again during the TFR. I informed the officers that I would contact our security office and my colleagues with drone licenses to inform them of the TFR and prevent this from happening again.When I returned to my office; I explored the situation further and was not initially finding clear information on the TFR for the area - as the FAA approved service 'Airspace Link' showed the TFR in effect Day 1 - Day 4 in local time. I then searched for the TFR map via the FAA and found additional information that was not present on the Airspace Link site including an earlier TFR on Day 0. This NOTAM report also specified the effective time window falling within my flight starting on Day 1. This is especially relevant as I was approved for a flight following the same procedures earlier in the week on Day 1 that began prior to the UTC time listed via the Airspace Link site but would be another incident with the TFR according to the local time start listed on the FAA NOTAM. While the flight on Day 1 also did not result in any takeoff warning via DJI's 'Before You Fly' map nor the drone's geofencing advisory warning system; it did not result in any incident with authorities on site at that date and time.Regardless of the details and circumstances around the TFR; I have greatly learned from this event as an exercise in following best practices and attention to detail; as well as cross-referencing information as important as flight zones. This experience has taught me to not be too comfortable with flight zones I am familiar with; and to rely on my own research and information prior to a flight for any special circumstances that may affect normal flight operation rather than drone alerts and the reliance of our internal security team to relay flight information. As a result of this experience; I will be certain to check both FAA NOTAMs and TFR maps; in addition to the FAA approved resources such as Airspace Link as close to launch as possible. Furthermore; following this incident I have already completed and received certificates for official supplemental rules and safety courses via faasafety.gov including 'Airspace; Special use Airspace and TFRs' and 'sUAS: Regulations; Laws; Airspace Ownership and FAA Enforcement;' and intend to continue refreshing my Airman knowledge with further supplemental coursework. I have also begun conversations with my organization's safety and security team to implement TFR check information into the pre-flight reporting procedure in order to reinforce the habit of checking for TFRs and more effectively communicate these potential risks to the rest of the organization; as there are a few other drone pilots within the organization. These discussions have already begun between our organization's drone pilots; helping to strengthen our community and awareness of flight safety and responsibility.

column121: In Month 6; prior to conducting a flight operation in Class E airspace; a Remote Pilot in Command (RPIC) performed a routine review of the documentation required for waivered flight operations. During this review; the RPIC discovered that the aircraft registration sticker was not attached to the drone and the registration card was missing from the drone case.The RPIC then verified the aircraft's registration status through the FAA DroneZone portal and determined that the registration had been marked as 'Cancelled' effective Month 0. As a result; the RPIC immediately suspended the planned flight operation and did not operate the aircraft.To prevent further use; the RPIC placed the drone and its remote controller into storage; labeled both the drone and its case as 'UNREGISTERED;' and removed the aircraft from service pending further investigation.The subsequent investigation revealed that the drone had been operated despite the cancelled registration. The aircraft registration was cancelled in Month 0 and was in storage until Month 3. Starting in Month 3; three different RPICs had conducted a total of 204 flights accumulating 67 flight hours using the aircraft over a period of approximately four months. The majority of these flights occurred in Class G (uncontrolled) airspace; while several flights were conducted in Class B (controlled) airspace after obtaining proper authorization through the Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability (LAANC) system. Although all required airspace approvals and clearances had been obtained for operations in controlled airspace; the aircraft's FAA registration was not in compliance during this period.The aircraft was initially operated by an experienced RPIC with several years of company drone operations experience. The drone was subsequently transferred in Month 4 to a new RPIC for their first inspection assignment. In Month 6; the drone was later handed off to another experienced RPIC. That RPIC performed maintenance but did not check registration documents upon receiving the aircraft. After approximately one week of operation; the final RPIC recognized that the aircraft's external FAA registration-number sticker was missing and initiated a review that ultimately identified a missing registration card and the cancelled registration status.The investigation determined that the registration had been cancelled in error due to a mislabeled drone case. A retired and damaged drone had been stored in a case incorrectly labeled with the identifier of an active operational drone. As a result; the FAA registration associated with the operational aircraft was mistakenly cancelled.The investigation also identified weaknesses in the drone registration management process. Registration documents were typically stored inside drone cases and were not readily visible during routine equipment checks; making it unlikely that a missing registration card would be immediately detected. Additionally; while the FAA registration sticker was missing from the aircraft; a company issued Drone Identifier sticker remained affixed to the drone. The presence of this identifier created the appearance that the aircraft was properly labeled; causing the absence of the FAA registration number sticker to go unnoticed during pre-flight inspections and routine use.Apparent Cause 1 Mislabeled drone case containing a damaged drone led to the cancellation of the registration of an operational active drone.Apparent Cause 2Registration cards are often kept inside drone cases underneath equipment to keep them secure. The registration cards are not readily visible to the RPICs leading UAS crews to inadvertently overlook the missing registration card.Corrective Actions:1) Conduct a safety stand-down to verify inventory and confirm all active drones have valid FAA registration.2) Update Uncrewed Aerial Systems (UAS) Fleet Management document to include recommended procedures for retired drones.3) Amend the Preflight Checklist to require drone registration validation and part of daily pre-flight checks.4) Attach a durable external registration tag to all active drone cases.5) Require all UAS crews to verify their assigned drone registration is present and current.6) Contact FAA regarding possible DroneZone inventory management improvements.7) Designate a single individual responsible for drone inventory management.8) Require maintenance log including drone registration verification be complete before operation in the field upon transferring drones between operators.9) Verify all active drones have FAA registration number sticker properly displayed on external surface of the aircraft.

column121: I secured local university permission to fly UAS/UAV on the university campus in advance of flights for XA:00 to XC:00/XD:00 on Day 0.  This is part of weekly planned flights on campus for flight practice/training hours for one student and learning in an independent study for another student. In addition to the educational outcomes; we fly to collect video and images for various business purposes on campus. On this particular day only one of the two students was present and flying as part of the planned flight; Person A. While Person A was manipulating the controls at the time with the Mavic 2 Pro; I was serving as Remote PIC. In addition to the Remote PIC; I also served as the Visual Observer.  Partly to assist with keeping an eye on the UAS/UAV; to assist with people who may be approaching nearby to the flight; and also to answer questions when individuals approach (common on a university campus). We typically meet at XA:00 and do pre-flight checks inside the office and then go out to fly. This particular morning; I was running late to meet at the office and this particular human factor led to me forgetting to do the TFR check as part of the pre-flight checklist.  I also did not ask if my student had checked. Come to find out; this turned out to be a very good learning experience for both of us and I doubt that either of us will ever forget to do that check again.  Our series of flights started at Location X on campus; then we flew in the area around Location Y and the area around Location Z. Our final flights to capture video and images for a campus project were to fly the east end of Location Z and Location A. We were approached multiple times during all of our flights and we paused flight; grounded the UAS/UAV; and ensured the safety of all passerby's whether walking or biking on campus. Flights were planned to be fairly low (below 100 feet and some at average height level of a human. The highest flight that we planned to fly was no more than 400 feet AGL and that was simply to ensure that the student had the experience of what that type of height is like from an observational experience. Our highest flights were along Location Z at 397 feet for less than 1-2 minutes. The drone at all times was above myself and the student manipulating controls; we didn't fly it beyond our line of sight and manually straight up from take off location(s) at the ends of Location Z. We were approached by several people during our flights that day asking questions from curiosity to technical questions. I handled most of the questions while Person A collected the images/video and maintained line of site. We were never further apart than about 10-15 feet and could communicate by voice without any issue. Both of us were in high visibility safety vests.  While not required; we find it's best to ensure others know we are flying our UAS for university business purposes as students are not allowed to fly on our campus unless part of a class or another business purpose.  At roughly XC:00; just after bringing the Mavic 2 Pro down from the west end of Location Y safely (literally we hovered in the air to ensure several families and people with dogs passed by before we landed); we began walking and preparing for the next flight -- the backside of Location A.  We were approached by an individual. He asked if we were with the university. I turned toward him with my name tag on and stated yes and explained our learning purpose and university business purpose of shooting videos. I thought he was a typical tourist asking questions or maybe a hobbyist or other Part 107 pilot. He then asked if we had checked the TFRs for the day and location and I realized I had not before we left. He then introduced himself as a law enforcement officer and flipped out his identification wallet.  I immediately opened my phone and app and realized we had unknowingly been flying just inside of a TFR.  The law enforcement officer acknowledged that they were aware of ourprevious flights that were just outside of the TFR and that we were brought to their attention only with our last flight that was just inside the edge of the radius of the area covered by the TFR. We immediately stopped all flights and began to put away the UAS. We discussed how this will be a good learning experience for my future classes and how I am often asked the question 'who enforces TFRs?'.  It truly was a mistake and we were not intending to break any TFRs when we set out for the filming and flights. We now have a printed checklist that must be checked through before leaving the office to ensure situational awareness.  Both Person A and I will NEVER forget to check TFRs.  I also notified our campus police (the entity that approves flights on our campus) and let them know that for the rest of that week the TFR was in place and flights should be avoided in the area we were in plus several of the university areas that are more administrative/facilities related.  This will be a discussion topic for our next drone committee meeting on campus; as we may want to use our UAS/UAV listserv to remind folks about active TFR's in the area of the university.
column123: I was flying a UAV (DJI Mavic 2 Pro) between XA:00 and XC:00 on Day 0 on campus; where I am a student. I was flying with Person B. Person B was serving as the remote PIC and visual observer; while I was the person manipulating controls. We were taking photo and video for the university to use in various business purposes on campus.While preparing to fly that day; I made the mistake of assuming that Person B had checked for TFRs; and as a result I neglected to do so myself; focusing on batteries and other set up duties. We made several flights around campus; covering Location X and Location Y. We mostly stayed under 100ft; but on our last flight we took the UAV up to 397ft AGL for practice and to get some more panoramic shots of campus. After our last flight of the day by Location A; we were approached by someone who identified themselves as a law enforcement officer and asked if we had checked the TFRs for the day. At that point we realized that we had both forgotten to. We packed up for the day.As a new pilot; this was a valuable learning experience. I understand now that I need to personally check TFRs before flying rather than rely on anyone else to do it. After this incident; I've made a checklist of items I need to perform before each flight and I plan to refer to it before each flight to ensure I don't miss anything.
